title: Professor Unrat
author: Heinrich Mann
source: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/35264 (Project Gutenberg, from the Kurt Wolff Verlag edition, Leipzig)
orthography: modernised to current German spelling (dass, muss, riss, ...) and current comma rules around quotations; wording unchanged
intro_en: Heinrich Mann (1871–1950), the older brother of Thomas Mann, wrote this satire about a small-town grammar-school teacher whom all his pupils secretly call 'Unrat' (rubbish, filth) instead of his real name, Raat. The novel is set in a classroom full of teenagers who play tricks on a bitter, power-hungry teacher – so the situations will feel familiar even though the school is from 1900. It was later filmed as 'The Blue Angel' with Marlene Dietrich. The narrator's German is dense, but the classroom scenes are full of real school slang and dialogue.

units.de: Da er Raat hieß, nannte die ganze Schule ihn Unrat. Nichts konnte einfacher und natürlicher sein. Der und jener Professor wechselten zuweilen ihr Pseudonym. Ein neuer Schub Schüler gelangte in die Klasse, legte mordgierig eine vom vorigen Jahrgang noch nicht genug gewürdigte Komik an dem Lehrer bloß und nannte sie schonungslos bei Namen. Unrat aber trug den seinigen seit vielen Generationen, der ganzen Stadt war er geläufig, seine Kollegen benutzten ihn außerhalb des Gymnasiums und auch drinnen, sobald er den Rücken drehte.
units.en: Since his name was Raat, the whole school called him Unrat. Nothing could be simpler or more natural. Now and then one professor or another changed his nickname. A new batch of pupils would arrive in the class, gleefully expose some funny feature of the teacher that last year's lot hadn't made enough of, and name it without mercy. Unrat, however, had carried his for many generations; the whole town knew it, and his colleagues used it outside the grammar school and inside too, as soon as he turned his back.
units.explain_en: The joke of the whole book: the teacher is called Raat, and 'Unrat' means rubbish or filth, so the pupils just added 'Un-'. 'Da' at the start of a sentence means 'since/because' (not 'there'). 'Professor' was the title of a senior teacher at a German 'Gymnasium' back then; today he would just be 'Lehrer' or 'Herr Raat'. 'den seinigen' is old for 'seinen' (his one). 'Pseudonym' here means nickname – today 'Spitzname'.

units.de:
Die Herren, die in ihrem Hause Schüler verpflegten und sie zur Arbeit anhielten, sprachen vor ihren Pensionären vom Professor Unrat. Der aufgeweckte Kopf, der den Ordinarius der Untersekunda hätte neu beobachten und nochmals abstempeln wollen, wäre nie durchgedrungen; schon darum nicht, weil der gewohnte Ruf auf den alten Lehrer noch so gut seine Wirkung übte wie vor sechsundzwanzig Jahren. Man brauchte nur auf dem Schulhof, sobald er vorbeikam, einander zuzuschreien:
»Riecht es hier nicht nach Unrat?«
Oder:
»Oho! Ich wittere Unrat!«
units.en:
The gentlemen who took in pupils as boarders and made them do their homework talked about 'Professor Unrat' in front of their lodgers. Any bright spark who might have wanted to take a fresh look at the form teacher of the Year 10 class and give him a new label would never have succeeded – if only because the old name still worked on the old teacher just as well as it had twenty-six years ago. All you had to do was shout to each other in the schoolyard as he walked past:
'Doesn't it smell of Unrat in here?'
Or:
'Oho! I can smell Unrat!'
units.explain_en: The nickname is so old that it is part of the town. 'Ordinarius' is an old word for the class teacher – today 'Klassenlehrer'. 'Untersekunda' is an old name for a school year (roughly Year 10 / tenth grade). 'Man brauchte nur ... zu' = you only had to ... – still normal: 'Du brauchst nur zu fragen.' 'Riecht es hier nach ...?' = does it smell of ... here? 'wittern' = to scent, like an animal; today 'riechen'.

units.de: Und sofort zuckte der Alte heftig mit der Schulter, immer mit der rechten, zu hohen, und sandte schief aus seinen Brillengläsern einen grünen Blick, den die Schüler falsch nannten, und der scheu und rachsüchtig war: der Blick eines Tyrannen mit schlechtem Gewissen, der in den Falten der Mäntel nach Dolchen späht. Sein hölzernes Kinn mit dem dünnen, graugelben Bärtchen daran klappte herunter und hinauf. Er konnte dem Schüler, der geschrien hatte, »nichts beweisen« und musste weiterschleichen auf seinen magern, eingeknickten Beinen und unter seinem fettigen Maurerhut.
units.en: And immediately the old man's shoulder twitched violently, always the right one, the one that sat too high, and from his glasses he shot a sideways green glance which the pupils called sly, but which was shy and vengeful: the look of a tyrant with a guilty conscience, searching the folds of people's coats for daggers. His wooden chin with its thin, greyish-yellow little beard dropped down and snapped shut. He couldn't 'prove anything' against the pupil who had shouted, and had to slink on, on his skinny, knock-kneed legs and under his greasy bricklayer's hat.
units.explain_en: A mean but funny description of Unrat. 'zucken' = to twitch. 'falsch' about a person means two-faced, sly. 'ein schlechtes Gewissen haben' = to have a guilty conscience – very common today. 'nichts beweisen können' = not to be able to prove anything; it's in quotation marks because it's Unrat's favourite phrase. 'magern' is an old short form of 'mageren' (skinny).

units.de:
Zu seiner Jubelfeier im Vorjahr hatte das Gymnasium ihm einen Fackelzug gebracht. Er war auf seinen Balkon getreten und hatte geredet. Während alle Köpfe, in den Nacken gelegt, zu ihm hinaufsahen, war plötzlich eine unschöne Quetschstimme losgegangen:
»Da ist Unrat in der Luft!«
Andere hatten wiederholt:
»Unrat in der Luft! Unrat in der Luft!«
Der Professor dort oben fing an zu stottern, obwohl er den Zwischenfall vorausgesehn hatte, und sah dabei jedem der Schreier in den geöffneten Mund. Die andern Herren standen in der Nähe; er fühlte, dass er wieder einmal »nichts beweisen« könne; aber er merkte sich alle Namen.
units.en:
For his anniversary the year before, the school had held a torchlight procession for him. He had stepped out onto his balcony and given a speech. While all heads were tipped back looking up at him, suddenly an ugly squashed-sounding voice had gone off:
'There's Unrat in the air!'
Others had repeated:
'Unrat in the air! Unrat in the air!'
The professor up there began to stammer, although he had expected this incident, and looked into the open mouth of each of the shouters. The other teachers were standing nearby; he felt that once again he 'couldn't prove anything'; but he memorised every name.
units.explain_en: Even at Unrat's big celebration the pupils mock him. This part is told in the Plusquamperfekt ('hatte gebracht', 'war getreten') because it happened before the main story. 'fing an zu stottern' = started to stammer ('anfangen zu' + infinitive). 'sich etwas merken' = to remember/make a note of something: 'Merk dir das!' 'vorausgesehn' is Mann's shortened form of 'vorausgesehen'.

words.en: to talk, to give a speech
to remember, to take note of

units.de: Schon tags darauf gab der mit der gequetschten Stimme dadurch, dass er das Heimatsdorf der Jungfrau von Orleans nicht kannte, dem Professor Gelegenheit zu der Versicherung, er werde ihm im Leben noch oftmals hinderlich sein. Richtig war dieser Kieselack zu Ostern nicht versetzt worden. Mit ihm blieben die meisten in der Klasse zurück von denen, die am Jubiläumsabend geschrien hatten, so auch von Ertzum. Lohmann hatte nicht geschrien und blieb dennoch sitzen. Dieser erleichterte die Absicht Unrats durch seine Trägheit und jener durch seine Unbegabtheit.
units.en: The very next day the boy with the squashed voice didn't know the home village of Joan of Arc, and so gave the professor the chance to assure him that he would stand in his way many more times in life. Sure enough, this Kieselack had not been moved up at Easter. Most of those in the class who had shouted on the anniversary evening were kept back with him, including von Ertzum. Lohmann had not shouted, but was kept back all the same. Lohmann made Unrat's plan easy through his laziness, von Ertzum through his lack of talent.
units.explain_en: Unrat takes revenge through grades. 'versetzt werden' = to be moved up to the next school year; 'sitzen bleiben' = to repeat a year – both still used in German schools today. 'die Jungfrau von Orleans' is Joan of Arc, and also the title of a play by Schiller that the class is studying. 'Dieser ... jener' = the latter ... the former. 'von' in 'von Ertzum' shows he's from a noble family.

Nächsten Spätherbst nun, an einem Vormittag um elf, in der Pause vor dem Klassenaufsatz über die Jungfrau von Orleans, geschah es, dass von Ertzum, der der Jungfrau immer noch nicht nähergetreten war und eine Katastrophe voraussah, in einem Anfall schwerfälliger Verzweiflung das Fenster aufriss und aufs Geratewohl, mit wüster Stimme in den Nebel hinausbrüllte:
»Unrat!«
units.en:
Now, the following late autumn, one morning at eleven, in the break before the class essay on Joan of Arc, it happened that von Ertzum – who still hadn't got to know Joan any better and could see a disaster coming – in a fit of clumsy despair tore open the window and, at random, bellowed wildly into the fog:
'Unrat!'
units.explain_en: The main story begins. 'die Pause' = break between lessons. 'der Aufsatz' = essay – a word every German pupil knows. 'geschah es, dass ...' = it happened that ... (today: 'passierte es, dass ...'). 'aufs Geratewohl' = at random, just on the off chance – still used, but 'einfach so' is more everyday. 'der Nebel' = fog.

units.de: Es war ihm unbekannt, ob der Professor in der Nähe sei, und es war ihm gleichgültig. Der arme, breite Landjunker war nur von dem Bedürfnis fortgerissen worden, noch einen kurzen Augenblick seinen Organen freies Spiel zu gewähren, bevor er sich für zwei Stunden hinhocken musste vor ein weißes Blatt, das leer war, und es mit Worten bedecken aus seinem Kopf heraus, der auch leer war.
units.en: He didn't know whether the professor was nearby, and he didn't care. The poor, broad young country squire had simply been carried away by the need to give his lungs free play for one brief moment before he had to squat down for two hours in front of a white sheet of paper that was empty, and cover it with words out of his head, which was empty too.
units.explain_en: Von Ertzum just needed to scream before a hard exam – very relatable. 'Es war ihm gleichgültig' = he didn't care; today you'd say 'Es war ihm egal' – 'Das ist mir egal!' is one of the most common phrases in German. 'ob der Professor in der Nähe sei' uses Konjunktiv I for reported thought. 'das Blatt' = sheet of paper (also: leaf). The joke: both the paper and his head are empty.

Kein Schüler hielt sich drunten auf, keinem konnte von Ertzum das Wort zugerufen haben. »Dieses Mal«, dachte Unrat frohlockend, »hat er mich gemeint. Diesmal kann ich es ihm beweisen!«
units.en: But in fact Unrat was just crossing the yard. When the shout from the window hit him, he gave an awkward jump. Up in the fog he made out von Ertzum's knobbly outline. There were no pupils down below; von Ertzum couldn't have been shouting the word at anyone else. 'This time,' Unrat thought triumphantly, 'he meant me. This time I can prove it!'

'droben' and 'drunten' are old/southern for 'oben' and 'unten'. 'Dieses Mal' and 'diesmal' both mean 'this time'. 'meinen' = to mean someone: 'Meinst du mich?' = Do you mean me?

units.de: »Es ist mir da vorhin immer mal wieder ein Wort zugerufen worden, eine Bezeichnung – ein Name denn also: ich bin nicht gewillt, ihn mir bieten zu lassen. Ich werde diese Schmähung durch solche Menschen, als welche ich Sie kennenzulernen leider Gelegenheit hatte, nie dulden, merken Sie sich das! Ich werde Sie fassen, wo immer ich es vermag.
units.en: 'Just now a word was repeatedly shouted at me, a label – a name, then, in short: I am not willing to put up with it. I shall never tolerate this insult from people such as I have unfortunately had occasion to get to know you as – mark my words! I shall catch you wherever I am able.'
units.explain_en: Unrat's speeches are deliberately pompous and full of filler words – Mann makes fun of how he talks, so don't copy this style! 'sich etwas bieten lassen' = to put up with something – still common: 'Das lasse ich mir nicht bieten!' = I won't stand for that! 'Merken Sie sich das!' = Remember that! (formal 'Sie'). 'denn also' is empty filler; normal German would be 'also'. 'dulden' = to tolerate.

units.de: Ihre Verworfenheit, von Ertzum, nicht genug damit, dass sie mir Abscheu einflößt, soll sie an der Festigkeit eines Entschlusses wie Glas zerbrechen, den ich Ihnen hiermit verkünde. Noch heute werde ich von Ihrer Tat dem Herrn Direktor Anzeige erstatten, und was in meiner Macht steht, soll – traun fürwahr – geschehen, damit die Anstalt wenigstens von dem schlimmsten Abschaum der menschlichen Gesellschaft befreit werde!«
units.en: 'Your depravity, von Ertzum – not only does it fill me with disgust, it shall also shatter like glass against the firmness of a decision which I hereby announce to you. This very day I shall report your deed to the headmaster, and everything in my power shall – verily and forsooth – be done so that the school may at least be freed from the worst scum of human society!'

Hierbei schwoll Unrats Stimme unterirdisch an.
»Sie sind nicht würdig, an der erhabenen Jungfrauengestalt, zu der wir jetzt übergehen, Ihre geistlose Feder zu wetzen. Fort mit Ihnen ins Kabuff!«
Von Ertzum, langsam von Verständnis, lauschte noch immer. Vor angestrengter Aufmerksamkeit ahmte er unbewusst mit den Kiefern die Bewegungen nach, die der Professor mit den seinigen vollführte. Unrats Kinn, in dessen oberem Rand mehrere gelbe Gräten staken, rollte, während er sprach, zwischen den hölzernen Mundfalten wie auf Geleisen, und sein Speichel spritzte bis auf die vorderste Bank. Er schrie auf:
»Sie haben die Kühnheit, Bursche!... Fort, sage ich, ins Kabuff!«
units.en:
At this, Unrat's voice swelled up from somewhere underground.
'You are not worthy to sharpen your brainless pen on the sublime figure of the Maid, to whom we now turn. Off with you into the cupboard!'
Von Ertzum, slow to understand, was still listening. In his strained attention he unconsciously copied with his jaws the movements the professor was making with his. Unrat's chin, in whose upper edge several yellow fish bones were stuck, rolled between the wooden folds of his mouth as he spoke, as if on rails, and his spit sprayed as far as the front desk. He shrieked:
'You have the nerve, boy!... Off, I say, into the cupboard!'
units.explain_en: Unrat sends von Ertzum to the 'Kabuff' – a dark little cloakroom used as punishment. 'Kabuff' is still used today in colloquial German for a tiny, poky room. 'würdig' = worthy. 'Fort mit Ihnen!' = Get out! (today: 'Raus!'). 'nachahmen' = to imitate. 'der Speichel' = spit. 'Bursche' (lad, boy) sounds old and insulting here; 'Junge' would be normal today.

Aufgescheucht drängte von Ertzum sich aus der Bank hervor. Kieselack raunte ihm zu:
»Mensch, wehr dich doch!«
Lohmann, dahinter, verhieß unterdrückt:
»Lass nur, den kriegen wir noch wieder kirre.«
Der Verurteilte trollte sich am Katheder vorbei, in das Gelass, das der Klasse als Garderobe diente, und worin es stockfinster war. Unrat stöhnte vor Erleichterung, als hinter dem breiten Menschen sich die Tür geschlossen hatte.
»Nun wollen wir die Zeit nachholen«, sagte er, »die uns dieser Bursche gestohlen hat. Angst, hier haben Sie das Thema, schreiben Sie es an die Tafel.«
units.en:
Startled, von Ertzum pushed his way out of his desk. Kieselack muttered to him:
'Come on, man, stand up for yourself!'
Lohmann, behind him, promised under his breath:
'Forget it, we'll get him tamed again yet.'
The condemned boy shuffled off past the teacher's desk into the little room that served as the class cloakroom and was pitch dark inside. Unrat groaned with relief when the door had closed behind the big lad.
'Now let us make up the time,' he said, 'that this fellow has stolen from us. Angst, here is the topic – write it on the board.'

'Lass nur' = Leave it / Don't worry. 'kriegen' is the everyday word for 'bekommen' (to get). 'jemanden kirre kriegen' = to tame someone, make them obedient (colloquial, a bit old). 'Angst' here is a pupil's surname! 'die Tafel' = the board; 'das Thema' = topic.

units.de:
Der Primus nahm den Zettel vor seine kurzsichtigen Augen und machte sich langsam ans Schreiben. Alle sahen mit Spannung unter der Kreide die Buchstaben entstehn, von denen so viel abhing. Wenn es nun eine Szene betraf, die man zufällig nie »präpariert« hatte, dann hatte man »keinen Dunst« und »saß drin«. Aus Aberglaube sagte man, noch bevor die Silben an der Tafel einen Sinn annahmen:
»O Gott, ich fall' rein.«
Schließlich stand dort oben zu lesen:
»Johanna: Es waren drei Gebete, die du tatst; Gib wohl acht, Dauphin, ob ich sie dir nenne!«
(Jungfrau von Orleans, erster Aufzug, zehnter Auftritt.)
»Thema: Das dritte Gebet des Dauphins.«
units.en:
The top boy held the slip of paper up to his short-sighted eyes and slowly started writing. Everyone watched tensely as the letters appeared under the chalk – so much depended on them. If it was about a scene you happened never to have 'prepared', then you 'hadn't a clue' and 'were stuck'. Out of superstition people said, even before the syllables on the board made any sense:
'Oh God, I'm done for.'
Finally, up there, it read:
'Joan: There were three prayers that you prayed; Take care, Dauphin, whether I name them to you!'
(The Maid of Orleans, Act One, Scene Ten.)
'Topic: The Dauphin's third prayer.'

Pupil slang in quotation marks: 'keinen Dunst haben' = to have no clue (today 'keine Ahnung haben'), 'drinsitzen' = to be in trouble, 'reinfallen' = to fall for it / be caught out. 'ich fall' rein' drops the -e, as in speech. The quote is from Schiller's play 'Die Jungfrau von Orleans'.

When they had read this, they all looked at each other. Because they were all 'stuck'. Unrat had 'caught them out'. With a crooked smile he sat down in the armchair on the platform and leafed through his notebook.

»Sie haben noch fünfviertel Stunden«, bemerkte Unrat gleichmütig, während er innerlich jubelte. Dieses Aufsatzthema hatte noch keiner gefunden von den unbegreiflich gewissenlosen Schulmännern, die durch gedruckte Leitfäden es der Bande ermöglichten, mühelos und auf Eselsbrücken die Analyse jeder beliebigen Dramenszene herzustellen.
Manche in der Klasse erinnerten sich des zehnten Auftritts im ersten Aufzug und kannten beiläufig die zwei ersten Gebete Karls. Vom dritten wussten sie nichts mehr, es war, als hätten sie es nie gelesen. Der Primus und noch zwei oder drei, darunter Lohmann, waren sogar sicher, sie hätten es nie gelesen.
units.en:
'You have an hour and a quarter left,' Unrat remarked calmly, while inwardly he was rejoicing. None of those incredibly unscrupulous schoolmasters had found this essay topic yet – the ones who, with their printed study guides, made it possible for the rabble to produce an analysis of any drama scene effortlessly, using cribs.
Some in the class remembered Scene Ten of Act One and roughly knew Charles's first two prayers. About the third they knew nothing any more; it was as if they had never read it. The top boy and two or three others, Lohmann among them, were even sure they had never read it.

units.de: Der Dauphin ließ sich ja von der Prophetin nur zwei seiner nächtlichen Bitten wiederholen; das genügte ihm, um an Johannas Gottgesandtheit zu glauben. Das dritte stand schlechterdings nicht da. Dann stand es gewiss an einer andern Stelle oder ergab sich irgendwo mittelbar aus dem Zusammenhang; oder es ging gar ohne Weiteres in Erfüllung, ohne dass man wissen konnte, hier ging etwas in Erfüllung? Dass es einen Punkt geben konnte, wo er niemals aufgemerkt hatte, das gab auch der Primus Angst im Stillen zu. Auf alle Fälle musste über dieses dritte Gebet, ja selbst über ein viertes und fünftes, wenn Unrat es verlangt hätte, irgendetwas zu sagen sein.

units.en: Years of German essays had trained them to cover a certain number of pages with empty phrases about things whose existence they were anything but convinced of – devotion to duty, say, or the blessings of school, or the love of military service. units.de: Mit der Jungfrau von Orleans beschäftigte die Klasse sich seit Ostern, seit dreiviertel Jahren. Den Sitzengebliebenen war sie sogar schon aus dem Vorjahr geläufig. Man hatte sie vor- und rückwärts gelesen, Szenen auswendig gelernt, geschichtliche Erläuterungen geliefert, Poetik an ihr getrieben und Grammatik, ihre Verse in Prosa übertragen und die Prosa zurück in Verse. Für alle, die beim ersten Lesen Schmelz und Schimmer auf diesen Versen gespürt hatten, waren sie längst erblindet. Man unterschied in der verstimmten Leier, die täglich wieder einsetzte, keine Melodie mehr.
units.en: The class had been working on The Maid of Orleans since Easter – for nine months. Those who'd been kept back even knew it from the year before. They had read it forwards and backwards, learned scenes by heart, supplied historical notes, done poetics on it and grammar, turned its verses into prose and the prose back into verse. For everyone who had felt a glow and shimmer on these verses at first reading, they had long since gone blind. In the out-of-tune droning that started up again every day, you couldn't make out any melody any more.

'seit dreiviertel Jahren' = for three quarters of a year; note German uses 'seit' + present tense for things still going on ('Ich lerne seit zwei Jahren Deutsch'). units.de: Niemand vernahm die eigen weiße Mädchenstimme, in der geisterhafte, strenge Schwerter sich erheben, der Panzer kein Herz mehr deckt, und Engelflügel weit ausgebreitet, licht und grausam dastehn. Wer von diesen jungen Leuten später einmal unter der fast schwülen Unschuld jener Hirtin gezittert hätte, wer den Triumph der Schwäche in ihr geliebt hätte, wer um die kindliche Hoheit, die vom Himmel verlassen, zu einem armen, hilflos verliebten kleinen Mädel wird, je geweint hätte, der wird nun das alles nicht so bald erleben. Zwanzig Jahre vielleicht wird er brauchen, bis Johanna ihm wieder etwas anderes sein kann als eine staubige Pedantin.
units.en: No one heard the strangely white girl's voice in which ghostly, stern swords rise up, armour no longer covers a heart, and angels' wings stand spread wide, bright and cruel. Whoever among these young people might later have trembled at the almost sultry innocence of that shepherd girl, whoever might have loved the triumph of weakness in her, whoever might ever have wept for the childlike majesty that, abandoned by heaven, becomes a poor, helplessly lovesick little girl – he will not experience any of that for a long time now. Perhaps he will need twenty years before Joan can be anything other to him than a dusty pedant.
units.explain_en: The hardest passage so far – the narrator mourns what school has destroyed: the chance to love great literature. Don't worry about every word. units.de: Die Federn kritzelten; Professor Unrat lugte, mit nichts weiter beschäftigt, über die gebeugten Nacken hinweg. Es war ein guter Tag, an dem er einen »gefasst« hatte, besonders wenn es einer war, der ihm »seinen Namen« gegeben hatte. Dadurch ward das ganze Jahr gut. Leider hatte er schon seit zwei Jahren keinen der heimtückischen Schreier mehr »fassen« können. Das waren schlechte Jahre gewesen. Ein Jahr war gut oder schlecht, je nachdem Unrat einige »fasste« oder ihnen »nichts beweisen« konnte.
units.en: The pens scratched away; Professor Unrat, with nothing else to do, peered over the bent necks. It was a good day when he had 'caught' someone, especially if it was one who had given him 'his name'. That made the whole year a good one. Unfortunately, for two years now he hadn't been able to 'catch' any of the sneaky shouters. Those had been bad years. A year was good or bad depending on whether Unrat 'caught' some of them or 'couldn't prove anything' against them.
units.explain_en: We see Unrat's twisted way of measuring success. 'jemanden fassen/erwischen' = to catch someone – today 'erwischen' is the normal word: 'Der Lehrer hat mich erwischt!' 'ward' is an old form of 'wurde' (became). 'lugen' is old for 'gucken/spähen' (to peek). 'je nachdem' = depending on – very useful: 'Je nachdem, wie das Wetter ist.'

units.de: Unrat, der sich von den Schülern hinterrücks angefeindet, betrogen und gehasst wusste, behandelte sie seinerseits als Erbfeinde, von denen man nicht genug »hineinlegen« und vom »Ziel der Klasse« zurückhalten konnte. Da er sein Leben ganz in Schulen verbracht hatte, war es ihm versagt geblieben, die Knaben und ihre Dinge in die Perspektive des Erfahrenen zu schieben. Er sah sie so nah, wie einer aus ihrer Mitte, der unversehens mit Machtbefugnissen ausgestattet und aufs Katheder erhoben wäre.
units.en: Unrat, who knew that the pupils attacked, cheated and hated him behind his back, for his part treated them as sworn enemies – you could never catch out enough of them or keep enough of them from reaching 'the class goal'. Since he had spent his whole life in schools, he had never been able to see boys and their affairs from the perspective of an experienced adult. He saw them as close up as one of their own would – one who had suddenly been given power and raised up onto the teacher's desk.
units.explain_en: The narrator explains why Unrat acts like a bully: he never grew up and fights the kids as if he were one of them. 'hinter jemandes Rücken / hinterrücks' = behind someone's back. 'der Feind, die Feinde' = enemy; 'Erbfeind' = arch-enemy. 'Knaben' is old-fashioned for 'Jungen' (boys). 'verbringen' = to spend (time) – 'Ich verbringe viel Zeit am Handy.'

units.de: Er redete und dachte in ihrer Sprache, gebrauchte ihr Rotwälsch, nannte die Garderobe ein »Kabuff«. Er hielt seine Ansprachen in dem Stil, den auch sie in solchen Fällen angewendet haben würden, nämlich in latinisierenden Perioden und durchwirkt mit »traun fürwahr«, »denn also« und ähnlichen Häufungen alberner kleiner Flickworte, Gewohnheiten seiner Homerstunde in Prima; denn die leichten Umständlichkeiten des Griechen mussten alle recht plump mitübersetzt werden.
units.en: He spoke and thought in their language, used their slang, called the cloakroom a 'Kabuff'. He gave his speeches in the very style they themselves would have used in such cases, namely in Latin-style long sentences, woven through with 'verily, forsooth', 'then, in short' and similar heaps of silly little filler words – habits from his Homer lessons with the top class, because every slight long-windedness of the Greek had to be clumsily translated along with it.
units.explain_en: Now we understand Unrat's weird speeches: he copies the clumsy style of schoolboys translating ancient Greek (Homer). 'Rotwälsch' (usually 'Rotwelsch') is thieves' slang; here it just means pupil slang – today you'd say 'Jugendsprache'. 'das Füllwort/Flickwort' = filler word, like 'like' or 'basically' in English. 'Prima' was the name for the top two years of school.

units.de: Da er selber steife Gliedmaßen bekommen hatte, verlangte er das Gleiche von den andern Insassen der Anstalt. Das fortwährende Bedürfnis in jugendlichen Gliedern und in jugendlichen Gehirnen, in denen von Knaben, von jungen Hunden – ihr Bedürfnis zu jagen, Lärm zu machen, Püffe auszuteilen, wehzutun, Streiche zu begehn, überflüssigen Mut und Kraft ohne Verwendung auf nichtsnutzige Weise loszuwerden: Unrat hatte es vergessen und nie begriffen.
units.en: Since his own limbs had grown stiff, he demanded the same from the other inmates of the institution. The constant need in young limbs and young brains – in those of boys, of young dogs – the need to chase about, make noise, hand out punches, hurt someone, play pranks, and get rid of surplus courage and energy in useless ways: Unrat had forgotten it and had never understood it.
units.explain_en: Unrat forgets that teenagers need to move and let off steam. 'verlangen' = to demand. 'das Gleiche' = the same. 'Lärm machen' = to make noise. 'wehtun' = to hurt: 'Das tut weh!' = That hurts! 'Streiche spielen' (Mann: 'begehn') = to play pranks – 'ein Streich' is a prank. 'Insassen' (inmates) makes the school sound like a prison – that's the point.

units.de: Wenn er strafte, tat er es nicht mit dem überlegenen Vorbehalt: »Ihr seid Rangen, wie's euch zukommt, aber Zucht muss sein«; sondern er strafte im Ernst und mit zusammengebissenen Zähnen. Was in der Schule vorging, hatte für Unrat Ernst und Wirklichkeit des Lebens. Trägheit kam der Verderblichkeit eines unnützen Bürgers gleich, Unachtsamkeit und Lachen waren Widerstand gegen die Staatsgewalt, eine Knallerbse leitete Revolution ein, »versuchter Betrug« entehrte für alle Zukunft.
units.en: When he punished, he didn't do it with the relaxed attitude of someone above it all: 'You're rascals, as boys should be, but there has to be discipline'; instead he punished in deadly earnest and with gritted teeth. What happened in school had, for Unrat, all the seriousness and reality of life. Laziness was as bad as being a useless citizen, inattention and laughter were resistance against the authority of the state, a cap-gun banger started a revolution, and 'attempted cheating' brought dishonour for all time.
units.explain_en: For Unrat, school is a small state and he is its dictator. 'strafen/bestrafen' = to punish; 'die Strafe' = punishment. 'Rangen' is old for naughty kids; today 'Frechdachse' or 'Rotzlöffel'. 'Zucht muss sein' = there must be discipline (today 'Disziplin muss sein'). 'mit zusammengebissenen Zähnen' = with gritted teeth. 'der Betrug' = cheating, fraud – 'bei der Klausur schummeln' is how pupils say 'cheat in a test'.

units.de: Aus solchen Anlässen erbleichte Unrat. Schickte er einen ins »Kabuff«, war ihm dabei zumute, wie dem Selbstherrscher, der wieder einmal einen Haufen Umstürzler in die Strafkolonie versendet und, mit Angst und Triumph, zugleich seine vollste Macht und ein unheimliches Wühlen an ihrer Wurzel fühlt. Und den aus dem »Kabuff« Zurückgekehrten und allen andern, die ihn je angetastet hatten, vergaß Unrat es nie. Da er seit einem Vierteljahrhundert an der Anstalt wirkte, waren Stadt und Umgegend voll von seinen ehemaligen Schülern, von solchen, die er bei Nennung seines Namens »gefasst« oder denen er es »nicht hatte beweisen« können, und die alle ihn noch jetzt so nannten!
units.en: On such occasions Unrat turned pale. When he sent someone into the 'Kabuff', he felt like an autocrat who once again sends a bunch of rebels off to a penal colony and at the same time, with fear and triumph, feels both his fullest power and an eerie burrowing at its roots. And Unrat never forgave those who came back from the 'Kabuff', or anyone else who had ever touched him. Since he had worked at the school for a quarter of a century, the town and the surrounding area were full of his former pupils – ones he had 'caught' when they said his name, or ones he 'hadn't been able to prove it' against – and all of them still called him that!

(today: 'er fühlte sich wie ...'). 'jemandem etwas nie vergessen' = never to forgive someone for something. 'ehemalig' = former: 'meine ehemalige Schule'. 'das Vierteljahrhundert' = quarter century.

units.de:
Die Schule endete für ihn nicht mit der Hofmauer; sie erstreckte sich über die Häuser ringsumher und auf alle Altersklassen der Einwohner. Überall saßen störrische, verworfene Burschen, die »ihr's« nicht »präpariert« hatten und den Lehrer befeindeten. Ein Neuer, noch ahnungslos, bei dem zu Haus ältere Verwandte über den Professor Unrat gelacht hatten wie über eine Jugenderinnerung von freundlicher Komik, und der nun mit dem Schub zu Ostern in Unrats Klasse gelangt war, konnte sich bei der ersten falschen Antwort anfauchen hören:
»Von Ihnen habe ich hier schon drei gehabt. Ich hasse Ihre ganze Familie!«
units.en:
For him, school didn't end at the wall of the yard; it spread out over all the houses around and over the inhabitants of every age. Everywhere sat stubborn, depraved lads who hadn't 'prepared' 'their bit' and were hostile to the teacher. A new boy, still unsuspecting, whose older relatives at home had laughed about Professor Unrat as a fond, funny memory from their youth, and who had now come into Unrat's class with the Easter intake, might find himself snapped at after his first wrong answer:
'I've already had three of you here. I hate your whole family!'
units.explain_en: A final shocking line that shows how personal Unrat's hate is. 'ahnungslos' = clueless, unsuspecting (from 'die Ahnung' – 'keine Ahnung!'). 'die Verwandten' = relatives. 'zu Haus' is a short form of 'zu Hause' (at home). 'die falsche Antwort' = the wrong answer. 'anfauchen' = to hiss/snap at (like a cat). 'Ich hasse ...' = I hate ...

units.en: While the class writes its essay, Unrat sits high up at his desk and feels safe – but new trouble is already on its way, from Lohmann. Lohmann is von Ertzum's best friend. He is seventeen and has had to repeat two school years; he is pale, with a black lock of hair falling over his forehead, writes poems in the style of Heinrich Heine and reads his own books under the desk. He looks at Unrat with bored contempt and never calls him by his nickname, which Unrat feels is even more insulting. Unrat hates him almost more than all the others. Lohmann usually protects the slow von Ertzum in class, so Unrat's attack on his friend's family makes him angry.

units.de:
Aber durch die Kränkung von Ertzums sah er sich persönlich herausgefordert. Er empfand, als der einzige unter dreißig, Unrats öffentliche Lebensbeschreibung des von Ertzumschen Onkels als eine niedrige Handlung. Zu viel durfte man dem Schlucker dort oben nicht erlauben. Lohmann entschloss sich also. Er stand auf, stützte die Hände auf den Tischrand, sah dem Professor neugierig beobachtend in die Augen, als habe er einen merkwürdigen Versuch vor, und deklamierte vornehm gelassen:
»Ich kann hier nicht mehr arbeiten, Herr Professor. Es riecht auffallend nach Unrat.«
units.en:
But the insult to von Ertzum made him feel personally challenged. He alone out of thirty felt that Unrat's public account of von Ertzum's uncle's life was a low thing to do. You couldn't let that poor wretch up there get away with too much. So Lohmann made up his mind. He stood up, leaned his hands on the edge of the desk, looked the professor in the eye with curious attention, as if he were about to carry out an interesting experiment, and declaimed in a calm, lordly voice:
'I can't work here any more, sir. There's a remarkable smell of Unrat.'
units.explain_en: Lohmann, the clever and arrogant pupil, decides to defend his friend. 'sich herausgefordert fühlen/sehen' = to feel challenged. 'als der einzige unter dreißig' = as the only one out of thirty. 'der Schlucker' (usually 'armer Schlucker') = poor devil – still used jokingly. 'Er entschloss sich' = he made up his mind; today also 'Er beschloss es'. The joke again: 'Es riecht nach Unrat' means both 'it smells of rubbish' and 'it smells of Unrat'.

units.de:
Unrat machte einen Sprung im Sessel, spreizte beschwörend eine Hand und klappte stumm mit den Kiefern. Hierauf war er nicht vorbereitet gewesen – nachdem er noch soeben einem Verworfenen die Relegation in Aussicht gestellt hatte. Sollte er nun auch diesen Lohmann »fassen«? Nichts wäre ihm erwünschter gekommen. Aber – konnte er es ihm »beweisen«?.. In diesem atemlosen Augenblick reckte der kleine Kieselack seine blauen Finger mit den zerbissenen Nägeln in die Höhe, knallte mit ihnen und keifte gequetscht:
»Lohmann lässt einen nicht ruhig nachdenken, er sagt immer, hier riecht es nach Unrat.«
units.en:
Unrat jumped in his chair, spread out one hand as if casting a spell and silently snapped his jaws. He hadn't been prepared for this – just after threatening a depraved boy with expulsion. Should he now 'catch' this Lohmann as well? Nothing would have pleased him more. But – could he 'prove' it?.. At that breathless moment little Kieselack stuck up his bluish fingers with their bitten nails, snapped them and squeaked in his squashed voice:
'Lohmann won't let a person think in peace, sir, he keeps saying it smells of Unrat in here.'
units.explain_en: Unrat's big problem is always whether he can 'prove' that someone said his name. The sneaky Kieselack pretends to complain about Lohmann – but in doing so he says the name too. 'vorbereitet sein auf' = to be prepared for. 'die Relegation' = expulsion from school (today: 'der Schulverweis'). 'Nichts wäre ihm erwünschter gekommen' = nothing would have been more welcome. 'keifen' = to squabble in a shrill voice. 'einen nicht in Ruhe lassen' is the modern form of 'einen nicht ruhig nachdenken lassen'.

units.de:
Es entstand Kichern, und einige scharrten. Da ward Unrat, der schon den Wind des Aufruhrs im Gesicht spürte, von Panik ergriffen. Er fuhr vom Stuhl auf, machte über das Pult hinweg eckige Stöße nach allen Seiten, wie gegen zahllose Anstürmende, und rief:
»Ins Kabuff! Alle ins Kabuff!«
Es wollte nicht ruhig werden; Unrat glaubte sich nur noch durch einen Gewaltstreich retten zu können. Er stürzte sich, ehe jener es vermuten konnte, auf Lohmann, packte ihn am Arm, zerrte und schrie erstickt:
»Fort mit Ihnen, Sie sind nicht länger würdig, der menschlichen Gesellschaft teilhaftig zu sein!«
units.en:
There was giggling, and some pupils scraped their feet. Unrat, who could already feel the wind of rebellion in his face, was seized by panic. He leapt up from his chair, made jerky pushing movements across the desk in all directions, as if against countless attackers, and shouted:
'Into the Kabuff! Everyone into the Kabuff!'
The class wouldn't calm down; Unrat believed only a violent stroke could save him now. Before Lohmann could guess what was coming, he threw himself at him, grabbed him by the arm, tugged and cried in a choked voice:
'Out with you, you are no longer worthy to belong to human society!'
units.explain_en: Unrat reacts like a dictator facing a revolution. The 'Kabuff' is the cloakroom next to the classroom used as a punishment room – today 'Kabuff' still means a tiny, dark room. 'ward' is the old past tense of 'werden' (today: 'wurde'). 'von Panik ergriffen' = seized by panic. 'packen' = to grab. 'teilhaftig sein' (+ genitive) is very formal/old = to share in; Unrat's pompous style is part of the joke.

units.en: Lohmann strolls calmly into the Kabuff, and Kieselack slips in after him. Unrat collects the three 'rebels'' exercise books. Lohmann has written only one cheeky page – and on the next, half-torn-out page Unrat finds the beginning of a poem: 'Homage to the great artiste Fräulein Rosa Fröhlich'. Unrat turns pink. That afternoon he reads the lines again and again and decides that Lohmann must be 'caught': if he can prove that the boy is involved with an actress, Lohmann will be finished at school. But first he has to find out who and where this Rosa Fröhlich is. Restless, he goes out into the cold rain. In town he sees a poster for Schiller's 'Wilhelm Tell' at the town theatre and goes there, nervously, to ask at the box office.

units.de:
Er stand schon eine Weile vor dem Fensterchen und räusperte sich leise. Als nichts erfolgte, pochte er an, mit der Spitze seines gekrümmten Zeigefingers. Der Kopf dahinter schrak in die Höhe und streckte sich sogleich aus dem zurückgeschobenen Schalter.
»Sie wünschen?«, fragte er heiser.
Unrat bewegte zuerst nur die Lippen. Sie sahen einander an, er und der abgedankte Schauspieler mit den tiefen, blauschwarzen Zügen, der flachen Nasenspitze und dem Klemmer darauf. Unrat brachte hervor:
»So? Sie geben denn also den Wilhelm Tell. Das ist recht von Ihnen.«
Der Kassierer sagte:
»Wenn Sie meinen, wir tun's zu unserm Privatvergnügen.«
units.en:
He had already been standing for a while in front of the little window, clearing his throat quietly. When nothing happened, he knocked with the tip of his crooked index finger. The head behind it jerked up and immediately poked out of the pushed-back hatch.
'Can I help you?' it asked hoarsely.
At first Unrat only moved his lips. They looked at each other, he and the retired actor with the deep, blue-black lines in his face, the flat tip of his nose and the pince-nez on it. Unrat managed to say:
'So? You are putting on Wilhelm Tell, then. That is good of you.'
The cashier said:
'If you think we do it for our own private amusement.'
units.explain_en: A very funny scene: the strict teacher is completely helpless outside his classroom. 'sich räuspern' = to clear one's throat. 'Sie wünschen?' = what can I do for you? – still used in shops, but today more often 'Was darf es sein?' or 'Kann ich Ihnen helfen?'. 'der Klemmer' = pince-nez (glasses clipped on the nose). 'etwas geben' can mean 'to perform' a play: 'Heute gibt man den Tell.' 'zu unserm Privatvergnügen' = for our own fun; 'unserm' = 'unserem'.

»Das habe ich Ihnen nicht unterstellen wollen«, versicherte Unrat, voll Angst vor Verwickelungen.
»Man verkauft ja nischt. Bloß, dass die klassischen Vorstellungen in dem Pachtvertrag drinstehn, den wir mit der Stadt haben.«
Unrat fand es geboten, sich bekannt zu geben.
»Ich bin nämlich der Professor Un– der Professor Raat, Ordinarius der Untersekunda am hiesigen Gymnasium.«
»Sehr angenehm. Mein Name ist Blumenberg.«
»Und ich würde recht gern mit meiner Klasse die Aufführung eines klassischen Dichterwerkes besuchen.«
units.en:
'I did not mean to suggest that', Unrat assured him, full of fear of complications.
'We don't sell a thing anyway. It's just that the classical performances are written into the lease we've got with the town.'
Unrat thought it proper to introduce himself.
'I am, you see, Professor Un– Professor Raat, form teacher of the Year 10 class at the grammar school here.'
'Pleased to meet you. My name is Blumenberg.'
'And I should very much like to attend a performance of a classical work of literature with my class.'
units.explain_en: Unrat almost says his own nickname ('Professor Un–')! 'unterstellen' = to suggest, to insinuate (something bad): 'Willst du mir etwas unterstellen?' 'nischt' is Berlin/northern slang for 'nichts'. 'drinstehn' = 'drinstehen' (to be written in). 'sich bekannt geben' is old; today 'sich vorstellen' (to introduce oneself). 'Sehr angenehm' = pleased to meet you – old-fashioned but still heard; today often 'Freut mich'.

»Ach, das ist aber ganz reizend von Ihnen, Herr Professor. Mit der Nachricht werd' ich bei unserm Direktor den größten Erfolg haben, da zweifle ich keinen Augenblick.«
»Aber«, und Unrat erhob den Finger, »es müsste – wahrlich doch – dasjenige von den Dramen unseres Schiller sein, das wir in der Klasse lesen, nämlich – immer mal wieder – die Jungfrau von Orleans.«
Der Schauspieler ließ die Lippen fallen, senkte den Kopf und sah von unten, mit Trauer und Vorwurf, zu Unrat auf.
units.en:
'Oh, that is really charming of you, Professor. That news will be a huge success with our director, I haven't a moment's doubt.'
'But', and Unrat raised his finger, 'it would have to be – truly now – the one of our Schiller's dramas that we are reading in class, namely – now and again – The Maid of Orleans.'
The actor let his lips droop, lowered his head and looked up at Unrat from below, full of sadness and reproach.
units.explain_en: Unrat uses his typical filler phrases: 'wahrlich doch' (truly), 'immer mal wieder' (now and again) – he says them even when they make no sense, which the author uses as a running joke. 'reizend' = charming (a bit old-fashioned). 'Ich zweifle keinen Augenblick' = I don't doubt it for a moment. 'Die Jungfrau von Orleans' is Schiller's play about Joan of Arc, which the class is reading. 'der Vorwurf' = reproach: 'Mach mir keine Vorwürfe!'

»Das tut mir aber fabelhaft leid. Weil wir die erst wieder einstudieren müssten, wissen Sie. Ist Ihnen wirklich mit 'm Tell nicht gedient? Der ist doch auch ganz hübsch für die Jugend.«
»Nein«, entschied Unrat, »das geht auf keinen Fall. Wir brauchen die Jungfrau. Und zwar käme es – aufgemerkt nun also! –«
Unrat schöpfte Atem, sein Herz klopfte.
»– ganz besonders auf die Darstellerin der Johanna an. Denn diese soll eine hehre Künstlerin sein, die den Schülern die erhabene Gestalt der Jungfrau – immer mal wieder – recht nahe bringt.«
units.en:
'I'm terribly sorry about that. Because we'd have to rehearse that one all over again, you know. Wouldn't Tell really do for you? It's quite nice for young people too.'
'No', Unrat decided, 'that is out of the question. We need the Maid. And what would matter – now pay attention! –'
Unrat took a breath, his heart was pounding.
'– most of all is the actress playing Joan. For she is to be a noble artiste, who brings the sublime figure of the Maid – now and again – really close to the pupils.'
units.explain_en: Now Unrat tries to steer the conversation towards Rosa Fröhlich. 'fabelhaft' normally means 'fabulous'; here it is used as an intensifier ('terribly'). 'einstudieren' = to rehearse, to learn (a play). 'mit etwas gedient sein' = to be helped by something – old; today 'Hilft Ihnen der Tell nicht?' 'Das geht auf keinen Fall' = that's absolutely not possible – very common today. 'aufgemerkt nun also!' is his classroom phrase for 'pay attention!' (today: 'Aufpassen!').

»Allerdings, allerdings«, sagte der Schauspieler, mit tiefem Einverständnis.
»Da habe ich denn nun an eine Ihrer Damen gedacht, die ich, und hoffentlich nicht mit Unrecht, auf das Höchste habe preisen hören.«
»Ach nee.«
»Nämlich an das Fräulein Rosa Fröhlich.«
»Wie, bitte?«
»Rosa Fröhlich«, und Unrat hielt die Luft an.
»Fröhlich? Haben wir ja gar nicht.«
»Wissen Sie das auch ganz genau?«, fragte Unrat, kopflos.
»Erlauben Sie, ich bin ja nicht meschugge.«
Unrat wagte den Mann nicht mehr anzusehn.
»Dann kann ich mir das aber gar nicht –«
units.en:
'Quite so, quite so', said the actor, with deep understanding.
'And so I thought of one of your ladies, whom I have heard praised most highly – and I hope not wrongly.'
'Oh really?'
'Namely Fräulein Rosa Fröhlich.'
'Pardon?'
'Rosa Fröhlich', and Unrat held his breath.
'Fröhlich? We haven't got one.'
'Are you quite sure of that?' asked Unrat, losing his head.
'Excuse me, I'm not meschugge.'
Unrat no longer dared to look at the man.
'But then I simply can't –'
units.explain_en: Unrat's plan fails: there is no Rosa Fröhlich at the theatre. 'Ach nee' is northern slang for 'Oh really?' ('nee' = 'nein'). 'Wie, bitte?' = Pardon? – today 'Wie bitte?'. units.en: The cashier helpfully suggests there must be a mix-up, and Unrat backs out, apologising – even when the man calls after him that they could still talk about tickets. Unrat wanders down to the harbour. There he walks into a shop for sailors and asks for a ticket for the summer theatre – in winter. The big red-bearded owner and the sailors think he is mad or making fun of them, and he is thrown out amid laughter. In the streets children on little carts shout 'Unrat!' after him, and former pupils grin at him instead of saying hello. Feeling that the whole town is a rebellious class of 'fifty thousand pupils', he flees to the quietest street at the edge of town. For the first time he feels a vague suspicion that the pupils have turned him into something bad over the years.

units.en:
He did not hear the conversation between two pupils from the very first generation, who stopped at a street corner and watched him go – mockingly, he thought:
'What's the matter with Unrat? He's getting old.'
'And dirtier and dirtier.'
'I've never known him any other way than dirty.'
'Oh, you probably don't remember. As a junior teacher he was still quite a neat fellow.'
'Really? What a name can do. I can't picture him clean at all.'
'Do you know what I think? Neither can he. Nobody can hold out against a name like that in the long run.'
units.explain_en: Two grown men who were Unrat's pupils long ago talk about him – not with hate, but with amused pity. The last line sums up the whole novel: the name 'Unrat' (rubbish) has shaped the man. 'immer schmutziger' = dirtier and dirtier ('immer' + comparative). 'adrett' = neat, smart – old-fashioned. 'sich etwas vorstellen' = to imagine something. 'gegen etwas ankönnen' = to be able to fight against something; today 'gegen so einen Namen kommt keiner an'. ''n' = 'ein/einen'.

units.en: Unrat suddenly remembers a colleague talking about the famous 'barefoot dancer Rosa Fröhlich' who was coming to town. The music shop that sells tickets has just closed, so he visits the pious shoemaker Rindfleisch, orders a pair of boots and tries to ask him about the dancer. But the shoemaker only talks about sin and angels. At home he can't concentrate on his life's work, a study of the little words (particles) in Homer, and rushes out again into the night. He creeps through the streets, looks up at windows and feels like 'an Indian on the warpath'. Down by the harbour he follows two workers to a big old house with a picture of a blue angel over the gate. Music is playing inside. On a poster at the door he reads a name that makes him break out in a sweat – and he plunges into the house.

Über dem Eingang rechts stand »Saal«; und dahinter war ein dumpfer Wirrwarr von Lauten, woraus manchmal ein sehr schriller hervorstach. Unrat zauderte, ehe er die Klinke drückte; er spürte darin eine Handlung, schwer von Folgen ... Ein sehr dicker, völlig unbehaarter kleiner Mann, der Bier trug, kam ihm entgegen. Er hielt ihn an.

units.en:
The hall was enormously wide and long, the honest hall of an old merchant's house, in which 'side matters' now went on. From a half-open door on the left came a rattling of pots and the glow of a fire. Over the entrance on the right was written 'Saal'; behind it was a muffled jumble of sounds, from which now and then a very shrill one stood out. Unrat hesitated before pressing the handle; he felt that this was an act heavy with consequences ... A very fat, completely bald little man carrying beer came towards him. He stopped him.
'Excuse me', he stammered, 'might I speak to the artiste Fröhlich?'
units.explain_en: Unrat enters the 'Blauer Engel' (Blue Angel), a sailors' tavern with a variety show. 'Nebendinge' ('side matters') is Unrat's word for everything that isn't schoolwork – here the author uses it ironically for entertainment and vice. 'zaudern' is old-fashioned for 'zögern' (to hesitate). 'die Klinke' = door handle. 'schwer von Folgen' = with heavy consequences. 'Wäre ... wohl zu sprechen?' is a very polite old way of asking 'Could I speak to ...?'

»Sie sind wohl der Herr Wirt zum Blauen Engel? Nun, das ist wahrlich recht brav. Ich bin nämlich der Professor Raat vom hiesigen Gymnasium und komme wegen eines Schülers, der hier zu finden sein soll. Können Sie mir vielleicht sagen, wo er ist?«
»Tjä, Herr Professer, denn gehn Sie man gleich 'n bischen in das Hinterzimmer zu die Künstlers, da sitzen die schungen Herrn jä immer ein.«

units.en:
'What d'you want to talk to her for?' asked the man. 'She's not talking now, she's singing. Have a listen.'
'You are the landlord of the Blue Angel, I suppose? Well, that is truly very commendable. I am, you see, Professor Raat of the grammar school here, and I have come on account of a pupil who is said to be here. Can you perhaps tell me where he is?'
'Well, Perfesser, then just you go straight into the back room to the artistes, that's where the young gentlemen always sit.'
'You see', said Unrat reprovingly, 'I thought as much. You must admit, man, that that is not in order.'

'Professer' is how he mispronounces 'Professor'. 'das Hinterzimmer' = back room. Unrat's 'Sehen Sie wohl' = 'You see?' 'in der Ordnung' – today we say 'in Ordnung' (okay, all right).

units.en: Unrat has to cross the hot, smoky hall, full of sailors, workers and soldiers who make fun of him. He sits down, drinks a beer and watches a brightly made-up singer on the little stage singing a silly song. Then he spots Kieselack laughing at him from a door beside the stage. As Unrat pushes through the crowd, his hat is knocked off, he spills a sailor's drink and bumps into a fat acrobat woman's collection plate. In a panic he shouts 'Into the Kabuff!' and chases Kieselack into the dressing room – but Kieselack and von Ertzum escape through the window. While Unrat is trying to climb up after them, a high voice behind him says: 'Come on, you're a strong young man!' He drops down and turns round: there stands the colourful woman from the stage.

units.de:
Unrat betrachtete sie eine Weile; seine Kiefern bewegten sich lautlos. Schließlich brachte er hervor:
»Sind Sie – demnach denn also – die Künstlerin Fröhlich?«
»Na ja«, sagte die Frauensperson.
Unrat hatte es gewusst.
»Und Sie führen Ihre Künste in diesem Gasthause vor?«
Auch dies wollte er noch von ihr selbst bestätigt hören.
»Originelle Frage«, bemerkte sie.
»Drum denn –«
Unrat schöpfte Luft; er wies hinter sich, nach dem Fenster, durch das Kieselack und von Ertzum entkommen waren.
»Sagen Sie mir – nun aber auch: dürfen Sie denn das?«
»Waschen?«, fragte sie erstaunt.
»Das sind Schüler«, sagte Unrat; und nochmals, mit Beben, tief aus der Brust:
»Das sind Schüler.«
units.en:
Unrat looked at her for a while; his jaws moved soundlessly. At last he managed to say:
'Are you – consequently then – the artiste Fröhlich?'
'Well, yes', said the woman.
Unrat had known it.
'And you perform your arts in this inn?'
He wanted to hear her confirm that too.
'Funny question', she remarked.
'Well then –'
Unrat took a breath; he pointed behind him, towards the window through which Kieselack and von Ertzum had escaped.
'Tell me – now then: are you allowed to do that?'
'Do what?' she asked, astonished.
'Those are pupils', said Unrat; and once more, trembling, from deep in his chest:
'Those are pupils.'

'Originelle Frage' = funny/odd question. 'Waschen?' is Rosa's slangy 'Was denn?' (What?), not 'to wash'! 'dürfen Sie denn das?' = are you even allowed to do that? 'die Frauensperson' is old and slightly contemptuous for 'woman' – today just 'die Frau'.

Die Künstlerin Fröhlich hörte auf zu lachen; sie richtete den Zeigefinger gegen ihre Brust.

»Oder wollen Sie etwa leugnen?«, fragte Unrat kampffertig.

units.en:
'For all I care. I don't get anything out of it.'
She laughed. Unrat burst out terribly.
'And you lure them away from school and from their duty! You are leading them astray!'
The artiste Fröhlich stopped laughing; she pointed her index finger at her own chest.
'Me? Is something wrong with you?'
'Or do you mean to deny it?' asked Unrat, ready for battle.
'Deny it to who? Thank God I don't need to. I'm an artiste, aren't I? Am I supposed to ask your permission whether gentlemen may give me bouquets?'

units.en:
She pointed to a corner where two big bouquets were stuck on the left and right of a forward-tilted dressing-table mirror. Shrugging:
'If a girl isn't even allowed to have that – say, who are you anyway?'
'I – I am the teacher', said Unrat, as if he were stating the meaning and law of the world.
'Well then', she said, making peace, 'then it can be just as much all the same to you as to me what the young people get up to.'
This philosophy of life found no way into Unrat's understanding.

'der Toilettenspiegel' = dressing-table mirror ('Toilette' here means getting dressed and made up, not WC). 'der Strauß, die Sträuße' = bouquet (also: ostrich!). 'die Schultern heben' = to shrug (today: 'mit den Schultern zucken'). 'pimpe' is Berlin slang for 'egal' (all the same). 'treiben' here = to get up to: 'Was treibst du so?'

Ich werde – fürwahr denn – dafür sorgen, dass sich mit Ihrem Treiben die Polizei beschäftigt.«
Bei diesem Wort erschien prompt die rückhaltloseste Verachtung auf dem Gesicht der Künstlerin Fröhlich.
»Wenn Sie mit der man nich selber was zu tun kriegen, Sie kommen mir ganz so vor. Ich bin mit der in Ordnung. Sie tun mir überhaupt leid, Sie!«

'I advise you', he said, 'to leave this town with your company, move off by long daily marches, for otherwise' – he raised his voice again – 'I shall do everything to make your career harder, if not impossible. I shall – verily – make sure that the police concern themselves with your activities.'
At this word the most unreserved contempt promptly appeared on the face of the artiste Fröhlich.
'Mind you don't have to deal with them yourself – you look just the type to me. I'm on good terms with them. I feel sorry for you, I do!'

'mit jemandem in Ordnung sein' = to be on good terms.

»Sie wollen sich noch aufspielen, in dem Aufzug wo Sie sind? Sie haben sich woll vorhin noch nich lächerlich genug gemacht? Gehn Sie mal hin, auf die Polizei, ja? Was meinen Sie, wenn ich mal einen von meine bekannten Herrn Offßiere auf Sie loslass? Sie werden ja einfach verkeilt.«
units.en:
But instead of pity she showed more and more clearly that she was angry.
'You still want to show off, in the state you're in? Haven't you made enough of a fool of yourself out there already? Go on, go to the police, why don't you? They'll arrest you on the spot. The tone the man takes! It seems very funny to someone who's used to the company of gentlemen. What do you think if I set one of my officer friends on you? You'll just get beaten up.'

'der Aufzug' here = outfit, state (today: 'in diesem Aufzug' = dressed like that). 'sich lächerlich machen' = to make a fool of oneself. 'Kavaliere' = gentlemen. 'verkeilen' is old slang for 'verprügeln' (to beat up).

units.en: Unrat is stunned: this woman isn't a pupil who can be punished, she is 'a foreign power', and he feels something like respect. The fat acrobats Kiepert and his wife Guste come in. They find him harmless, pour him some wine and even clean his dirty hat, and Unrat feels strangely warm among these people. Alone with Rosa, he watches her sew a costume and asks about his pupils. He describes Lohmann in detail; she pretends not to know him but reads his poem, which makes fun of her. Then she flirts with Unrat, says she prefers a mature man to silly boys, and tells him he must come back tomorrow or his pupils will get up to mischief. Kiepert leads him out. In the dark alley Unrat sees three figures leaning against the wall: Kieselack, von Ertzum and Lohmann.

units.de:
Unrat machte eine scharfe Wendung; hinter sich hörte er ein Schnaufen, das aus der breitesten der drei Brüste kommen musste, aus Ertzums Brust, und das nach Empörung klang. Da erscholl Kieselacks Quetschstimme:
»In dem Haus, wo eben einer rausgekommen is, soll es aber 'ne ganze Masse sittlichen Unrat geben.«
Unrat zuckte empor; vor Wut und Angst fletschte er die Zähne.
»Ich werde Sie alle zerschmettern. Morgen bringe ich – wahrlich doch! – das Geschehene zur Anzeige!«
Niemand antwortete. Unrat machte nochmals kehrt und schlich zwei, drei Schritte weiter, in einem drohenden Schweigen. Da, ganz langsam, sagte Kieselack, und Unrat zuckte bei jedem der zwei Worte mit dem Nacken:
»Wir auch!«
units.en:
Unrat turned sharply; behind him he heard a snort, which must have come from the broadest of the three chests, Ertzum's, and which sounded outraged. Then came Kieselack's squashed voice:
'In that house someone just came out of, they say there's a whole load of moral rubbish.'
Unrat started; he bared his teeth in rage and fear.
'I shall crush you all. Tomorrow – truly! – I shall report what has happened!'
Nobody answered. Unrat turned round again and crept two, three steps further, in a threatening silence. Then, very slowly, Kieselack said – and Unrat flinched at each of the two words:
'So will we!'
units.explain_en: The power balance changes: the boys have seen their teacher in the back room of a tavern, so they can report him too. 'sittlicher Unrat' = 'moral rubbish/filth' – another play on his name. 'die Empörung' = outrage. 'die Zähne fletschen' = to bare one's teeth. 'zerschmettern' = to smash, to crush. 'zur Anzeige bringen' = to report (to the authorities); today 'anzeigen' or 'melden'. 'Wir auch!' = So will we! / We will too!

units.en: The three boys go into the dressing room. Von Ertzum is madly in love with Rosa; Kieselack is secretly closer to her than the others know; Lohmann plays the bored, ironic observer – he is really in love with an older married woman, Dora Breetpoot, and writes sad poems about her. Next morning the boys fear Unrat will report them, but he says nothing, afraid they will tell what they saw. In the evening Unrat goes back to the Blue Angel early, telling himself he must keep Lohmann away. Unrat helps Rosa get ready for the stage and watches her sing 'Der Mond ist rund', a sentimental song Lohmann wrote. The audience laughs at it, and Unrat is furious – he feels Rosa is his business now. He orders champagne. Late at night Rosa suddenly cries: behind the glitter, she says, there is only grey misery.

units.de:
Sie jammerte noch weiter. Unrat suchte peinlich nach etwas, das er ihr sagen könne. Indes kam Kiepert von draußen, hob Unrat vom Stuhl und erklärte, ihn hinausgeleiten zu wollen. Unter der Tür hatte Unrat etwas gefunden. Er wendete sich, und seine Hand tastete durch die Luft, mit Anstrengung zurück nach der Künstlerin Fröhlich, die schon schlief, und versprach ihr:
»Ich werde versuchen, Sie durchzubringen.«
Dies konnte ein Lehrer vor der Versetzung zu einem Schüler sagen, dem er wohlwollte, oder er konnte es über ihn denken. Aber Unrat hatte es noch zu keinem gesagt und von keinem gedacht.
units.en:
She went on lamenting. Unrat searched awkwardly for something he could say to her. Meanwhile Kiepert came in from outside, lifted Unrat off his chair and announced that he would see him out. In the doorway Unrat had found something. He turned, and his hand groped through the air, with an effort, back towards the artiste Fröhlich, who was already asleep, and he promised her:
'I shall try to get you through.'
A teacher might say this to a pupil he was fond of before the end-of-year decision on who moves up, or he might think it about him. But Unrat had never yet said it to anyone, or thought it of anyone.
units.explain_en: A touching and funny moment: Unrat can only express kindness in school language. 'jemanden durchbringen' = to get someone through (an exam, into the next class). 'die Versetzung' = being moved up to the next school year – still used in German schools ('Die Versetzung ist gefährdet!'). 'jemandem wohlwollen' = to be well-disposed to someone (old). 'jammern' = to moan, to lament. 'peinlich' here = painfully, awkwardly; today mostly 'embarrassing'.

units.de: Es war Achteinviertel und Unrat noch immer nicht da. In der Gier, ihre Freiheit auszunutzen, lärmte die Klasse bis zur Selbstbetäubung, bis zur Verblödung. Alles schrie, ohne noch darum zu wissen, »Unrat! Unrat!« Die einen waren davon unterrichtet, er sei tot. Die andern schwuren, er habe seine Wirtschafterin zu Haus ins Kabuff gesperrt und sie verhungern lassen, und befinde sich zu dieser Stunde im Zuchthaus. Lohmann, Ertzum und Kieselack schwiegen dazu.
units.en: It was a quarter past eight and Unrat still wasn't there. Greedy to make use of their freedom, the class made a din until they were dazed, until they were stupid. Everyone was shouting 'Unrat! Unrat!' without even knowing it any more. Some had heard that he was dead. Others swore he had locked his housekeeper in the Kabuff at home and let her starve, and was at this very moment in prison. Lohmann, Ertzum and Kieselack said nothing.
units.explain_en: The next morning: Unrat is late for the first time in years, and the class goes wild with rumours. 'Achteinviertel' = viertel nach acht (8:15) – regional way of telling the time, still used in parts of Germany ('viertel neun' = 8:15 in the east/south). 'lärmen' = to make noise. 'die Wirtschafterin' = housekeeper (today: 'die Haushälterin'). 'das Zuchthaus' = old word for a prison with hard labour; today 'das Gefängnis'. 'schwören' = to swear.

units.en: Unrat creeps into class looking grey and tired and ignores the three boys – who now share a strange, frightening secret with him. At break Lohmann tells von Ertzum that Rosa fell asleep at the table after Unrat bought her champagne. From now on Unrat goes to the Blue Angel every evening, always before Lohmann can get there. He tidies the dressing room, sorts out Rosa's costumes and secretly learns to do her stage make-up, until one evening she lets him do her whole face.

units.de:
Einmal gab sie ihm sogar einen Backenstreich. Darauf zog sie hastig ihre Hand zurück, betrachtete sie, roch daran und versetzte starr:
»Sie sind ja fettig.«
Er errötete, hilflos. Und sie brach aus:
»Er schminkt sich! Nu schlag' einer lang hin! Darum hat er es so rasch herausgehabt. Er lernt es heimlich an sich selber! O Sie – Unrat!«
Unrat machte ein entsetztes Gesicht.
»Jawoll: Unrat!«
Sie tanzte um ihn her.
units.en:
Once she even slapped his face. Then she quickly pulled her hand back, looked at it, sniffed it and said, staring:
'You're all greasy.'
He blushed, helpless. And she burst out:
'He wears make-up! Well, I'll be blowed! That's why he picked it up so fast. He practises in secret on himself! Oh, you – Unrat!'
Unrat made a horrified face.
'That's right: Unrat!'
She danced around him.
units.explain_en: Rosa discovers that Unrat practises putting make-up on his own face – and calls him by his nickname. 'der Backenstreich' is old for 'die Ohrfeige' (slap). 'fettig' = greasy. 'sich schminken' = to put on make-up – very common today. 'Nu schlag' einer lang hin!' is a Berlin exclamation of surprise, like 'Well, I never!' (today maybe 'Das gibt's doch nicht!'). 'heraushaben' = to have figured out how to do something. 'Jawoll' = 'Jawohl' (yes indeed).

units.en: And Unrat smiles happily: it doesn't hurt him when Rosa calls him 'Unrat' – it feels almost like a pet name. 'Prost, Unrat,' she says, and admits she likes him more than the Kieperts, but asks: 'What do you actually want?' Unrat never thinks about that. He only worries about his three pupils. At night he waits for them outside the Blue Angel, walks them home 'to discuss the art they have enjoyed', criticises Lohmann's poem and makes sure each of them goes to bed. Von Ertzum is desperate: on a Sunday outing to a prehistoric burial mound (a 'Hünengrab'), which he damaged in wild high spirits, Rosa turned down his offer to run away with him. At the Blue Angel, Unrat now guards Rosa's dressing-room door. The regulars, who first mocked him, slowly start to respect him, but rumours about the old professor begin to spread through town.

units.de:
Ein junger Oberlehrer besuchte, unter dem Schutze des ältesten Professors, eines halbtauben Greises, den Blauen Engel und gewann Einblicke in die Wahrheit. Am nächsten Morgen im Lehrerzimmer sprach der taube Professor zu Unrat einige beschwörende Worte über die Würde des Erzieherstandes. Der junge Oberlehrer lächelte skeptisch. Die andern Herren sahen weg; mehrere zuckten die Achseln. Unrat erschrak: er sah sich vor einem schlechthin unglaublichen Eingriff in seine Machtvollkommenheit. Sein Kinn klappte; er brachte hervor:
»Das ist – traun fürwahr – nicht Ihre Sache.«
Er wendete sich nochmals um.
»Meine Würde – aufgemerkt nun also! – gehört mir selbst ganz allein.«
units.en:
A young senior teacher visited the Blue Angel under the protection of the oldest professor, a half-deaf old man, and gained insight into the truth. The next morning in the staff room, the deaf professor spoke a few urgent words to Unrat about the dignity of the teaching profession. The young teacher smiled sceptically. The other gentlemen looked away; several shrugged. Unrat was shocked: he saw himself faced with a simply unbelievable interference with his absolute power. His chin wobbled; he managed to say:
'That is – verily – none of your business.'
He turned round once more.
'My dignity – now pay attention! – belongs to me alone.'
units.explain_en: Unrat's colleagues find out and warn him – and he answers like a king. 'der Oberlehrer' was the title of a senior grammar-school teacher. 'das Lehrerzimmer' = staff room – still the normal word. 'die Würde' = dignity. 'mit den Achseln zucken' = to shrug. 'die Machtvollkommenheit' = absolute power (formal). 'Das ist nicht Ihre Sache' = that's none of your business – today often 'Das geht Sie nichts an'. 'traun fürwahr' = truly (extremely old-fashioned).

units.en: Unrat is angry that people dare to criticise him. Out of spite against the rich families Lohmann belongs to, he even goes with Kiepert to vote for the Social Democrats – although he has always supported the Kaiser and strict order. He grows jealous and suspicious whenever Rosa is out of his sight, and treats the Kieperts more and more rudely. Frau Kiepert warns Rosa that Unrat gives her nothing: no money and no love. To annoy the Kieperts after their patriotic navy song, Rosa sings a cheeky parody about a ship's captain who comes home drunk and hits his wife – and the audience loves it.

units.de:
Da trat Kiepert ein und schob vor sich her einen untersetzten Mann mit einem rötlichen Haarband rund um das rotfleischige Gesicht. Der zog die Brauen in die Höhe und sagte:
»Gottsdunner, Fräulein, Sie sind jä 'n dolle Deern, sind Sie jä. Huhu! Denn haut er mich auf'n – Ich bin nämlich auch 'n Kaptain, und wenn Sie was mit mich trinken wollen –«
Schon griff Unrat ein.
»Die Künstlerin Fröhlich trinkt – traun fürwahr – mit niemand. Da irren Sie, Mann. Überdies verkennen Sie sichtlich den privaten Charakter dieses Kab–, dieser Garderobe.«
units.en:
Then Kiepert came in, pushing in front of him a stocky man with a reddish fringe of beard all round his red, fleshy face. The man raised his eyebrows and said:
'Blimey, miss, you're a crazy lass, you are. Hoo-hoo! Then he hits me on the – I'm a captain too, you see, and if you'd like a drink with me –'
Unrat was already stepping in.
'The artiste Fröhlich drinks – verily – with nobody. You are mistaken there, man. Moreover you clearly misjudge the private character of this Kab–, this dressing room.'
units.explain_en: A real sea captain liked Rosa's cheeky song. He speaks Low German-flavoured slang: 'Gottsdunner' (a curse, like 'Blimey!'), 'jä' = 'ja', 'Deern' = girl ('Mädchen' in northern German), 'mit mich' instead of 'mit mir' (wrong case). 'eingreifen' = to step in, to intervene. 'Da irren Sie' = you are mistaken – still correct, a bit formal. Unrat almost says 'Kabuff' again. 'verkennen' = to misjudge.

»Mit nichten«, erklärte Unrat. »Vielmehr belehre ich Sie darüber, dass Sie hinausgehn müssen.«

Seine Frau brach endlich los:

'You're joking, mister', and the captain raised his eyebrows even higher.

Unrat war fahl, er zitterte.
»Die Künstlerin Fröhlich«, rief er mit einer Stimme aus der Tiefe und schielte giftig vor Angst nach ihr hin, »ist nicht eine Sobeschaffene, dass es ihr anstehen würde, Ihr Bier zu trinken, Mann!«
Sein Blick stach sie; sie seufzte.

Und Unrat im Triumph, plötzlich rot auf den Backenknochen, und mit einem Sprung:
»Hören Sie es, Mann? Sie sagt es Ihnen selbst. Die Künstlerin Fröhlich verweist Sie ins Exil. Gehorchen Sie! Vorwärts nun also!«
units.en:
Unrat was pale; he was trembling.
'The artiste Fröhlich', he cried in a voice from the depths, squinting at her venomously out of fear, 'is not the kind of person for whom it would be fitting to drink your beer, man!'
His look stung her; she sighed.
'Go away again, then', she said, 'there's nothing doing here.'
And Unrat, triumphant, suddenly red on his cheekbones, and with a leap:
'Do you hear it, man? She tells you so herself. The artiste Fröhlich sends you into exile. Obey! Now then, forward!'

'Gehorchen Sie!' = Obey! 'Vorwärts nun also!' = his classroom 'Come on, then!'

units.en: Unrat grabs the big captain and pushes him out of the door, and even Kiepert backs down. Frau Kiepert then tells Unrat plainly: the captain has money and likes Rosa, Rosa owes her 270 marks, and a young woman wants love, which Unrat simply 'doesn't think of'. Unrat, shaken, offers to pay for Rosa's lodging. Rosa shyly invites him to see her little room upstairs, and from that night on they are a couple. Kieselack spies through the keyhole and fetches the others; von Ertzum is heartbroken. The three boys then walk into the dressing room, where Unrat and Rosa sit together with champagne. Unrat, now the master of the Kabuff, orders von Ertzum to recite the hymn verses set for homework. When Kiepert laughs at him, von Ertzum furiously attacks the acrobat, and the two start wrestling on the floor.

Meanwhile Unrat, without granting the wrestling match more than a passing interest, had turned to Lohmann.
'But what about you, then, Lohmann? There you sit smoking – now and again – a cigarette; and this morning you were absent from class.'
'I wasn't in the mood, sir.'
'But for a visit to the Blue Angel you are – verily – always in the mood.'
'That's something different, sir. I had a migraine this morning. The doctor forbade me any mental effort and prescribed distraction.'
'I see. Be that as it may ...'
Unrat snapped his jaws a few times first. Then he had it.

Und da Lohmann nichts tat, als ihn hinter halb gesenkten Lidern hervor mit müder Neugier ansehn, brauste Unrat auf:

Lohmann ließ eine Weile verstreichen. Unterdessen taumelten Kiepert und Ertzum gegen den Tisch; Unrat musste sich selbst, die Künstlerin Fröhlich und mehrere Gläser und Flaschen in Sicherheit bringen. Als dies geschehen war:

'There you sit smoking', he repeated. 'Is that proper for a pupil in the presence of his teacher?'
And since Lohmann did nothing but look at him from under half-lowered lids with weary curiosity, Unrat flared up:
'Throw away that cigarette!' he shouted dully.
Lohmann let a moment pass. Meanwhile Kiepert and Ertzum staggered against the table; Unrat had to bring himself, the artiste Fröhlich and several glasses and bottles to safety. When that was done:
'Well! Come on, then!'
'The cigarette', replied Lohmann, 'belongs to the situation. The situation is unusual – for both of us, sir.'

'Throw that cigarette away, I say!'
'Sorry', said Lohmann.
'You would dare ...! You rascal!...'
Lohmann merely made an elegant, dismissive gesture with his pointed hand.
Then Unrat, seized by the giddiness of the threatened tyrant, leapt up from his chair.
'You will throw it away, or I shall hold you back in your career! I shall crush you! I am not inclined –!'
Lohmann shrugged.
'How regrettable, sir. All that is over now. That you can misunderstand the circumstances like that.'

units.en: Unrat then mocks Lohmann in front of everyone for his 'unhappy love' – and Rosa laughs too. Lohmann is shocked, believing they know about Dora Breetpoot, until he realises they only mean his old poem about Rosa. He leaves, humiliated but relieved. On the way home he tells von Ertzum that Unrat is becoming 'interesting': a kind of anarchist who doesn't care what anyone thinks of him. Unrat now pays for Rosa's meals and a hotel room, orders furniture for a flat for her and proudly says her name in every shop in town. Rosa refuses to be seen with him in public yet, afraid people will tell him stories about her past. At school, thanks to Kieselack, everybody knows about Unrat's private life. Some teachers stop greeting him, and one tells Unrat's own class to keep away from 'moral filth'.

units.de:
Wenn jetzt Unrat den Schulhof betrat, schrie, während der beaufsichtigende Lehrer angewidert wegsah, alles drauflos:
»Oho! Hier riecht es nach sittlichem Unrat!«
Der alte Professor näherte sich, der Lärm schwoll, unter Unrats giftigem Schielen, allmählich ab; dann stellte an seinem Wege sich Kieselack auf und versetzte mit einem Senkblick, langsam und nachdrücklich:
»Vielmehr Kot.«
Und Unrat schlich zusammenzuckend weiter; er konnte es Kieselack nicht beweisen.
units.en:
Now when Unrat entered the schoolyard, everyone started shouting, while the teacher on duty looked away in disgust:
'Oho! It smells of moral Unrat in here!'
The old professor came closer, and under Unrat's poisonous squint the noise slowly died down; then Kieselack placed himself in his path and said with a downward glance, slowly and emphatically:
'Or rather, filth.'
And Unrat crept on, flinching; he couldn't prove it against Kieselack.
units.explain_en: The pupils now use the teachers' own words against Unrat. A colleague had spoken of 'sittlicher Un–, vielmehr Kot' (moral Un–, or rather, filth); Kieselack repeats 'Vielmehr Kot'. 'der Schulhof' = schoolyard. 'drauflos schreien' = to start shouting away. 'angewidert' = disgusted. 'abschwellen' = to die down. 'vielmehr' = or rather. 'zusammenzucken' = to flinch. Unrat's old problem again: he can't 'prove' it.

units.en: Unrat has lost all power over the three boys: they know his secret, so they can do what they like. Lohmann refuses to take part in lessons, von Ertzum copies his neighbour's test, and Kieselack disrupts the class and starts fights. If Unrat locks them in the Kabuff, the class hears bottles being opened, toasts and giggling in there, and Unrat has to let them out quickly. But he doesn't really care: they are still the losers, because Unrat, not Lohmann, has Rosa. As soon as he leaves school he thinks only of her laundry and the sweets he wants to surprise her with.

units.de:
Dagegen konnte der Direktor des Gymnasiums nicht länger umhin, einzugreifen in die Zustände der Untersekunda. Er entbot Unrat zu sich ins Amtszimmer und hielt ihm die sittliche Auflösung vor, der seine Klasse sichtlich entgegengehe. Er wolle nicht untersuchen, woher der Ansteckungsstoff komme. Bei einem jüngeren Lehrer würde er dies allerdings untersuchen. Der Herr Kollege aber sei in Ehren ergraut, er möge daher einerseits seiner selbst gedenken, andererseits aber auch des Beispiels nicht vergessen, das er der Klasse schulde.
Unrat sagte darauf:
»Herr Direktor: der Athenienser Perikles hatte – traun fürwahr – die Aspasia zur Geliebten.«
Dies passe hier wohl nicht, meinte der Direktor. Und Unrat:
units.en:
The headmaster of the grammar school, however, could no longer avoid stepping in to deal with the state of the Year 10 class. He summoned Unrat to his office and pointed out to him the moral decay towards which his class was clearly heading. He did not wish to investigate where the infection came from. With a younger teacher he would, of course, investigate. But his colleague had grown grey with honour; he should therefore think of himself on the one hand, and on the other not forget the example he owed his class.
Unrat replied:
'Headmaster: Pericles the Athenian had – verily – Aspasia as his mistress.'
The headmaster said that hardly fitted here. And Unrat:
units.explain_en: The headmaster tries to warn Unrat politely, without saying directly what he means – and Unrat answers with ancient Greek history: Pericles, the great leader of Athens, lived with the educated courtesan Aspasia. Most of the headmaster's words are in indirect speech with Konjunktiv I: 'Er wolle nicht untersuchen' = he did not wish to investigate. 'nicht umhin können' = to be unable to avoid. 'das Amtszimmer' = office (today: 'das Büro'). 'in Ehren ergraut' = grown grey with honour. 'die Geliebte' = lover, mistress.
