»Ich würde mein Leben – immer mal wieder – für nichts erachten, wenn ich den Schülern die klassischen Ideale nur vorerzählte wie müßige Märchen. Der humanistisch Gebildete darf des sittlichen Aberglaubens der niederen Stände billig entraten.«
Der Direktor, der nicht weiter wusste, entließ Unrat und dachte noch lange nach. Zuletzt beschloss er, das Gehörte für sich zu behalten, aus Furcht, der Laie möchte es in einem für Schule und Lehrerstand unvorteilhaften Sinne auslegen.
units.en:
'I should consider my life – now and again – worth nothing if I merely told the pupils about the classical ideals like idle fairy tales. A person with a humanist education may reasonably do without the moral superstition of the lower classes.'
The headmaster, who didn't know what to say, dismissed Unrat and thought about it for a long time. In the end he decided to keep what he had heard to himself, for fear that ordinary people might interpret it in a way harmful to the school and the teaching profession.

'der Laie' = layperson, non-expert – still common: 'Als Laie verstehe ich das nicht.' 'für sich behalten' = to keep to oneself.

sentences.de: Zuletzt beschloss er, das Gehörte für sich zu behalten, aus Furcht, der Laie möchte es in einem für Schule und Lehrerstand unvorteilhaften Sinne auslegen.
sentences.en: In the end he decided to keep what he had heard to himself, for fear that ordinary people might interpret it in a way harmful to the school and the teaching profession.

units.en: Unrat's housekeeper walks out on him in protest against Rosa's visits. The pious shoemaker Rindfleisch comes to remind him of God's will, but Unrat only smiles and pushes him out. Then a scandal breaks: a forest warden reports that the prehistoric burial mound in the woods has been damaged by a group of young people. The headmaster promises that any pupil who names the culprits will go unpunished and even get a reward. A few days later Unrat triumphantly announces in class that Lohmann, Kieselack and von Ertzum will soon be leaving school 'in the company of common thieves'. The three are put on trial. Unrat waits on the witness bench with a poisonous smile. Kieselack denies everything; Lohmann and von Ertzum admit the damage but refuse to name anyone else who was there.

units.de:
»Es war also sonst keiner dabei?«, wiederholte der Vorsitzende.
»Nein«, sagte Ertzum.
»Nein«, sagte Lohmann.
»Doch!«, rief Kieselack im Quetschdiskant des beflissenen Schülers, der »seins« weiß. »Die Künstlerin Fröhlich war auch noch mit!«
Und da alles lauschte:
»Die hat es ja überhaupt bloß haben wollen, dass wir das Hünengrab ruinieren sollten.«
»Er lügt«, sagte Ertzum und knirschte.
»Er lügt bei jedem Wort«, ergänzte Lohmann.
»Es is so gewiss wahr!«, beteuerte Kieselack. »Fragen Sie man Herrn Professor! Der kennt sie am besten.«
units.en:
'So nobody else was there?' the presiding judge repeated.
'No', said Ertzum.
'No', said Lohmann.
'Yes!' cried Kieselack in the squashed treble of an eager pupil who 'knows his stuff'. 'The artiste Fröhlich was there too!'
And as everyone listened:
'She's the one who wanted us to wreck the burial mound in the first place.'
'He's lying', said Ertzum, grinding his teeth.
'He's lying with every word', added Lohmann.
'It's true, honest!' Kieselack insisted. 'Just ask the professor! He knows her best.'
units.explain_en: Kieselack takes his revenge: he drags Rosa – and so Unrat – into the court case. 'der Vorsitzende' = the presiding judge (still used). 'der Diskant' = treble (high voice). 'seins wissen' is school slang: to know one's lesson. 'das Hünengrab' = a prehistoric stone grave ('Hüne' = giant). 'ruinieren' = to ruin. 'lügen' = to lie. 'beteuern' = to insist, to assure.

Er grinste nach der Zeugenbank.
»Is es vielleicht nich wahr, dass Ihnen die Künstlerin Fröhlich an dem Sonntag durchgegangen is, Herr Professor? Da hat sie mit uns beim Hünengrab Frühstück gegessen.«
Alles blickte auf Unrat, der zerstört aussah, und dessen Kiefer klappten.
»War die Dame dabei?«, fragte einer der Richter überrascht und im Tone rein menschlicher Neugier die beiden andern Angeklagten. Sie hoben die Schultern. Aber Unrat brachte hervor, fast erstickt:
»Das ist Ihr Ende, Sie Elender! Rechnen Sie sich – immer mal wieder – zu den Toten!«
units.en:
He grinned towards the witness bench.
'Isn't it true that the artiste Fröhlich ran off from you that Sunday, Professor? She had breakfast with us by the burial mound.'
Everyone looked at Unrat, who looked shattered and whose jaws were snapping.
'Was the lady there?' one of the judges asked the other two defendants in surprise, in a tone of purely human curiosity. They shrugged. But Unrat brought out, almost choking:
'This is your end, you wretch! Count yourself – now and again – among the dead!'

'jemandem durchgehen' = to run away from someone (also used for horses). 'zerstört' = destroyed; here: shattered. 'der/die Angeklagte' = defendant – still the legal term. 'die Neugier' = curiosity. 'ersticken' = to choke, to suffocate. 'der Elende' = wretch. 'sich zu den Toten rechnen' = to count oneself among the dead.

units.en: Asked about his pupils, Unrat explodes in court: he calls the boys 'the future inmates of prison' and reveals all their secrets – Lohmann's poems, von Ertzum's night climbs, Kieselack's visits to the tavern – and insults their rich families. The court finds him ridiculous. Rosa is called as a witness. She looks elegant, admits she was on the outing, says one of the boys proposed marriage to her, and hints that she was close to Kieselack. Everyone laughs. Unrat slips out of the courtroom, heartbroken: for the first time in his life he feels betrayed, and in his imagination he sees Rosa with Lohmann. The next days he still goes to school, but his colleagues ignore him completely. The whole town talks about the trial, and old former pupils shake their heads when they see him in the street.

»Wer sich selber in seinen Jahren noch pikante Seitensprünge vorzuwerfen hat und öffentlich damit reinfällt. Er sitzt doch überhaupt in 'n Glashaus. In der Bürgerschaft soll die Geschichte zur Sprache kommen, und dass sie ihn nich mehr haben wollen bei der Schule, das weiß ich von Breetpoot. Er kann man wegziehn mit seiner Freundin.«
units.en:
'What's become of our old Unrat, I ask you. It's a crying shame, it is, the stories he's been getting up to lately.'
'A teacher doesn't act like that against a few lads. Is that supposed to be an educator of the young? And then his attacks on the business community and on the best families. In court, if you please.'
'A man who's still guilty of juicy little flings at his age and gets found out in public. He's living in a glass house anyway. They say the matter's going to be raised in the town council, and that they don't want him at the school any more, I know that from Breetpoot. He might as well move away with his girlfriend.'
units.explain_en: Respectable citizens gossip about Unrat in the street. Northern colloquial forms: 'is' = 'ist', ''n' = 'ein', 'nich' = 'nicht', 'denn' = 'dann', 'man' = just. 'der Jammer' = misery, pity ('Es ist ein Jammer' = it's a shame). 'der Seitensprung' = affair, fling – still very common. 'im Glashaus sitzen' comes from the proverb 'Wer im Glashaus sitzt, sollte nicht mit Steinen werfen' (people in glass houses shouldn't throw stones). 'die Bürgerschaft' = the town council of a Hanseatic city (like Hamburg or Lübeck today).

'But she's a fine lass.'

And the gentlemen smiled at each other, each with a little twinkle in his eye.

units.en: Some citizens who want to change society celebrate Unrat as a brave man who stood up to the rich, but he ignores their invitations. He sits at home thinking of Rosa with hate and longing, wishing she would leave town. Only at night does he walk round her hotel. There he meets Lohmann, who has come from outside Frau Breetpoot's house, and threatens to have him thrown out of school. Lohmann, who knows that Unrat's own dismissal has already been decided, feels sorry for the lonely old man.

units.de: Wenige Tage später hatten die schwebenden Schicksale sich gesenkt. Lohmann, dem nichts daran lag, durfte, bis er nach England ging, auf der Schule verbleiben; seine Verwandten waren zu mächtig, als dass an seine Entfernung zu denken gewesen wäre. Kieselack verdankte seinen Abschied nicht dem Vorfall mit dem Hünengrab; eher seiner ungebührlichen Aufführung vor Gericht; vor allem aber seinen zur Künstlerin Fröhlich unterhaltenen und von ihr bekannt gegebenen Beziehungen, die unzulässig erschienen für einen Sekundaner. Von Ertzum ging freiwillig und überantwortete sich einer Presse. Unrat ward entlassen.
units.en: A few days later the fates that had been hanging in the air came down. Lohmann, who didn't care about it, was allowed to stay at school until he went to England; his relatives were too powerful for anyone to think of removing him. Kieselack owed his departure not to the incident with the burial mound; rather to his improper behaviour in court; but above all to the relationship he had had with the artiste Fröhlich, which she had made public and which seemed unacceptable for a Year 10 pupil. Von Ertzum left of his own accord and handed himself over to a crammer. Unrat was dismissed.
units.explain_en: The results of the scandal – and the unfair difference between rich and poor pupils. 'schwebend' = hanging, pending. 'verbleiben' = to remain (formal). 'mächtig' = powerful. 'ungebührlich' = improper (old). 'unzulässig' = not permitted. 'freiwillig' = voluntarily – very common. 'die Presse' here is old slang for a private cramming school that prepares pupils for exams, not 'the press'! 'entlassen' = to dismiss, to fire – today also 'kündigen' or 'rauswerfen'.

units.en: Pastor Quittjens visits Unrat, offers to help him return to respectable society and tells him he must give up Rosa, because his example is poisoning the young people of the whole town. When the pastor insults Rosa, Unrat throws him out. But the pastor's words give him a dark idea: through Rosa he could take revenge on all his old 'pupils' in the town. He goes back to Rosa, and they make up. Rosa promises that she never loved Lohmann, and Unrat forbids her ever to see him again. A happy time begins: they sit in a theatre box and enjoy people's envious looks. Rosa, whom nobody has ever taken so seriously, starts to take herself seriously, tries hard to love Unrat and asks him to teach her Latin – then Greek, because it is harder.

units.de: Um den Misserfolg ihres Gefühls zu vergüten, nahm sie einige Male beim Griechischen allen ihren Verstand zusammen. Unrat rötete sich fleckig und eilte wonnebebend den Partikeln entgegen. Als er den Homer aufschlug und sie zum ersten Mal ein μὲν ... δὲ νῦν herauslesen ließ – als diese geliebten Laute nun wirklich aus dem bunten Gesicht der Künstlerin Fröhlich und von ihren anmutig bemalten Lippen fielen: da klopfte sein Herz. Er musste das Buch weglegen und sich sammeln.
units.en: To make up for the failure of her feelings, she a few times summoned all her intelligence for the Greek lessons. Unrat went red in patches and hurried, trembling with bliss, towards the particles. When he opened Homer and had her read out, for the first time, a 'men ... de nyn' – when these beloved sounds really fell from the colourful face of the artiste Fröhlich and from her charmingly painted lips: then his heart pounded. He had to put the book down and compose himself.
units.explain_en: The Greek particles in Homer are Unrat's life's work – hearing Rosa read them is the happiest moment of his life. 'vergüten' = to compensate (today: 'ausgleichen', 'wiedergutmachen'). 'der Misserfolg' = failure. 'den Verstand zusammennehmen' = to pull one's wits together. 'wonnebebend' = trembling with bliss (poetic). 'Homer aufschlagen' = to open (a book by) Homer. 'bemalt' = painted. 'sich sammeln' = to compose oneself.

units.de:
Seine Atmung war noch sehr in Unruhe; er nahm auf dem Tisch die kleine weiche und immer etwas fettige Hand der Künstlerin Fröhlich und sagte, er sei nicht gesonnen, sich auch nur für eine Stunde des ihm erübrigenden Lebens von ihr zu trennen. Er wolle sie heiraten.
Erst verzog sie den Mund zum Weinen. Darauf lächelte sie bewegt, lehnte ihre Wange an seine Schulter und wiegte sich darauf. Das Wiegen ward zum Zucken; ihr Jubel brach aus, sie riss Unrat vom Stuhl, schwenkte ihn umher.
»Nu wer' ich Frau Unrat! Ich lach' mir ja 'n Ast! Frau Professor Unrat – nee, Raat, bitte, meine Herrschaften.«
units.en:
His breathing was still very agitated; he took the artiste Fröhlich's small, soft and always slightly greasy hand on the table and said he was not inclined to be separated from her for even an hour of the life left to him. He wanted to marry her.
At first her mouth twisted as if to cry. Then she smiled, moved, leaned her cheek on his shoulder and rocked on it. The rocking turned to shaking; her joy burst out, she pulled Unrat up from his chair and swung him round.
'Now I'll be Frau Unrat! I'll laugh myself silly! Frau Professor Unrat – no, Raat, if you please, ladies and gentlemen.'
units.explain_en: Unrat proposes – in his usual formal indirect style: 'er sei nicht gesonnen ... Er wolle sie heiraten' (Konjunktiv I for reported speech). 'sich trennen von' = to separate from. 'heiraten' = to marry. 'den Mund verziehen' = to twist one's mouth. 'bewegt' = moved (emotionally). 'Ich lach' mir ja 'n Ast!' is slang for 'I'm killing myself laughing' – still used today. Rosa jokes that she'll be 'Mrs Rubbish'.

units.en: Rosa immediately plays at being the dignified wife of a professor and wants to move into Unrat's villa outside the town gate. But over the next days she seems distracted and worried, often goes out alone and gets impatient when Unrat wants to come. One day he sees her coming out of a cheap inn, and she only says mysteriously: 'Things aren't always the way some people think.'

units.de:
Eines weiteren Tages endlich trippelte, wie Unrat allein und betrübt durch die mittäglich leere Siebenbergstraße ging, ein kleines weißgekleidetes Kind auf ihn zu und sagte mit einem einfältigen Plärrstimmchen:
»Komm nach Haus, Papa.«
Unrat blieb erstaunt stehen und sah auf die kleine, weißbehandschuhte Hand, die das Kind ihm hinstreckte.
»Komm nach Haus, Papa«, wiederholte es.
»Was heißt nun das?«, fragte Unrat. »Wo wohnst du denn?«
units.en:
One day at last, as Unrat was walking alone and sadly along the Siebenbergstraße, empty at midday, a little child dressed in white toddled up to him and said in a simple, whiny little voice:
'Come home, Papa.'
Unrat stopped in astonishment and looked at the little hand in a white glove that the child was holding out to him.
'Come home, Papa', it repeated.
'Now what does that mean?' asked Unrat. 'Where do you live, then?'
units.explain_en: Rosa's secret is revealed in a sweet and clever way. 'trippeln' = to toddle, to take small quick steps. 'einfältig' = simple, naive. 'das Plärrstimmchen' = whiny little voice ('plärren' = to bawl, to whine – still used in southern German). 'nach Haus(e) kommen' = to come home. 'hinstrecken' = to hold out. 'Wo wohnst du denn?' – 'denn' in questions makes them sound more natural and friendly.

Unrat sah auf, und da erblickte er an der nächsten Ecke die Künstlerin Fröhlich, mit schmeichlerisch schiefem Köpfchen und mit einer halben Gebärde der Hand, die sich schüchtern ein Stückchen von der Hüfte weg bewegte, als entschuldigte sie und als bäte sie.

units.en:
'There', and it pointed behind itself.
Unrat looked up, and there at the next corner he saw the artiste Fröhlich, with her head coaxingly tilted to one side, and with half a gesture of her hand, which moved shyly a little way from her hip, as if she were apologising and as if she were begging.
Unrat snapped his jaws helplessly. All at once he had understood; and the little white-dressed hand that was still being held out to him – he simply took it.

units.en: The little girl, Mimi, is Rosa's daughter, and Unrat marries Rosa – boys throw stones at their carriage outside the registry office. The family spends the summer at the seaside, where rich men flirt with Rosa and give her presents, while Unrat quietly makes fun of them to her. Back home the money is soon gone: Unrat's savings have been spent on furniture, clothes and fun, and creditors send angry letters. So Unrat gives 'Greek lessons' to a former pupil, the wine merchant Lorenzen, who once shouted Unrat's name at their wedding. The lessons turn into parties in Unrat's villa with champagne, songs and more and more guests, and finally into card games for high stakes. Many young men lose a lot of money there. One night Rosa wins more than 12,000 marks as a dowry for Mimi – but the next morning creditors take it all.

Andererseits verbreitete sich das Gerücht, der Weinhändler Lorenzen stelle seine Zahlungen ein. Unrat lief sofort nach Erkundigungen, und wie er zurückkam, war er bleich, feucht, und konnte kein Wort hervorbringen. Schließlich, schnappend, mit klappenden Kiefern:
»Er macht Bankrott. Der Schüler Lorenzen macht Bankrott!«
»Was ich mir dafür kaufe«, erwiderte die Künstlerin Fröhlich, auf der Ottomane zusammengesunken und mit den Händen schaukelnd zwischen den Knien.
»Der Schüler Lorenzen macht Bankrott«, wiederholte Unrat. »Der Schüler Lorenzen liegt zerschmettert am Erdboden und wird sich nicht wieder erheben. Seine Laufbahn ist – traun fürwahr – jäh beendet.«
units.en:
On the other hand the rumour spread that the wine merchant Lorenzen was stopping his payments. Unrat immediately ran off to make enquiries, and when he came back he was pale and damp and couldn't get a word out. At last, gasping, his jaws snapping:
'He's going bankrupt. The pupil Lorenzen is going bankrupt!'
'A fat lot of good that does me', replied the artiste Fröhlich, slumped on the ottoman and swinging her hands between her knees.
'The pupil Lorenzen is going bankrupt', Unrat repeated. 'The pupil Lorenzen lies smashed on the ground and will not rise again. His career is – verily – suddenly at an end.'

'die Zahlungen einstellen' = to stop payments (a sign of bankruptcy). 'Erkundigungen einziehen' / 'sich erkundigen' = to make enquiries. 'Bankrott machen' = to go bankrupt; today 'pleitegehen' is very common. 'Was ich mir dafür kaufe' = 'what do I get for that?' – today 'Was habe ich davon?'. 'die Ottomane' = a kind of sofa.

units.en: Unrat's villa becomes the town's secret gambling club. Respectable men of every kind – merchants, officers, a consul, a police official, judges, even Pastor Quittjens – come to play and drink until morning, and Rosa flirts with many of them. Unrat is delighted every time one of his former 'pupils' is ruined: his enemy Dr Hübbenett discovers his own son gambling there but has to back down when he sees who else is present; a young man almost drowns when Rosa dares him to swim far out after a big meal; the young teacher Richter loses his rich fiancée because of Rosa. Gossip spreads through every family, businesses go bankrupt, and one ruined shopkeeper takes his own life. Unrat now calls himself proudly 'a real Unrat'.

units.de: Und diese Entsittlichung einer Stadt, von keinem zu unterbrechen, weil zu viele darin verwickelt waren: sie geschah durch Unrat und zu seinem Triumph. Seiner insgeheim ihn schüttelnden Leidenschaft – dieser Leidenschaft, von der sein trockner Körper nichts als hie und da ein giftig grünes Augenfunkeln, ein blasses Feixen entließ – ihr frondete und unterlag eine Stadt. Er war stark; er mochte glücklich sein.
units.en: And this moral corruption of a whole town, which no one could stop because too many were involved in it: it happened through Unrat and for his triumph. To his passion, which secretly shook him – this passion, of which his dry body let nothing out except now and then a poisonous green flash of the eyes, a pale sneer – to this passion a whole town slaved and succumbed. He was strong; he might well be happy.
units.explain_en: The narrator sums up Unrat's revenge: the whole town is corrupted. 'die Entsittlichung' = moral corruption (from 'die Sitte' = morals, custom). 'verwickelt sein in' = to be involved/entangled in. 'die Leidenschaft' = passion. 'feixen' = to smirk, to sneer – still used colloquially. 'fronen' = to slave away (from 'die Fron' = forced labour); 'frondete' is its past tense. 'unterliegen' = to succumb, to be defeated. 'mochte' here means 'might': 'Er mochte glücklich sein' = he may well have been happy.

units.en: But Unrat is not truly happy. He really loves Rosa, and every time she spends time with another man he suffers; he searches her things, hides in his room and imagines her with others – and in his jealous fantasies the other man always has Lohmann's face, although Lohmann left town long ago. Rosa goes along with the 'game', thinking it all can't be taken so seriously. When Unrat talks about retiring somewhere with their winnings, she tells him bitterly that they are deep in debt and nothing in the house really belongs to them; she only goes on for Mimi's sake. Then she makes it up to him again. On a sunny spring day the two walk into town together as friends and allies, smiling at the shopkeepers who shout after them about unpaid bills.

units.de:
In der Siebenbergstraße war eine Begegnung mit dem Möbelhändler auszuhalten, der behauptete, sie hätten von den noch nicht bezahlten Möbeln mehrere weiterverkauft, und mit dem Gericht drohte. Unrat forderte ihn giftig lächelnd auf, er möge doch nachsehn. Die Künstlerin Fröhlich äußerte:
»Da machen Sie sich man weiter keine Hoffnung drauf. So klug sind wir allein, dass da nischt Gutes bei zu holen is.«
In diesem Augenblick geschah neben ihr ein Säbelklirren. Sie sah hin und rasch wieder weg. Eine Stimme sagte rau:
»Donnerwetter!«
Und eine andere, gelassen verwunderte:
»Sieh mal an.«
units.en:
In the Siebenbergstraße they had to put up with meeting the furniture dealer, who claimed they had sold on several pieces of the furniture that hadn't been paid for yet, and threatened to go to court. Smiling poisonously, Unrat invited him to go and look. The artiste Fröhlich remarked:
'Don't get your hopes up. We're clever enough on our own that there's nothing good in it for you.'
At that moment a sabre clinked beside her. She glanced over and quickly away again. A voice said roughly:
'Good heavens!'
And another, calmly surprised:
'Well, look at that.'
units.explain_en: Two old acquaintances are back in town – the next unit tells us who. 'aushalten' = to put up with, to bear. 'der Möbelhändler' = furniture dealer. 'weiterverkaufen' = to sell on. 'mit dem Gericht drohen' = to threaten legal action. 'sich Hoffnung machen' = to get one's hopes up. 'das Säbelklirren' = the clinking of a sabre (a soldier's sword) – so one of the men is now an officer. 'Donnerwetter!' is still used as an exclamation of surprise. 'Sieh mal an' = well, look at that.

units.de: Die Künstlerin Fröhlich hörte nicht mehr, was der Möbelhändler redete. Nach einer Weile ließ sie ihn stehen. Sie ging weiter in einer leichten Betäubung. Erst gegenüber dem Konditor Mumm fiel ihr auf, dass auch Unrat nichts mehr sagte. Sie fühlte etwas wie schlechtes Gewissen und fing harmlos zu sprechen an, im Drang, ihn nach dem, was sie soeben erblickt hatten, wieder zu versöhnen. Auch er war plötzlich von erregter Herzlichkeit und lud sie zum Konditor ein. Während er am Büfett bestellte, ging sie schon ins Nebenzimmer. Da ward an die Scheibe geklopft. Sie hütete sich, hinzusehn; sie wusste auch so, das waren wieder Ertzum und Lohmann.
units.en: The artiste Fröhlich no longer heard what the furniture dealer was saying. After a while she left him standing there. She walked on in a slight daze. Only opposite Mumm's cake shop did she notice that Unrat wasn't saying anything either. She felt something like a bad conscience and started chatting harmlessly, anxious to reconcile him after what they had just seen. He too was suddenly full of excited warmth and invited her into the cake shop. While he was ordering at the counter, she was already going into the side room. Then someone knocked on the window. She took care not to look; she knew anyway that it was Ertzum and Lohmann again.
units.explain_en: Lohmann and von Ertzum have returned – and both Rosa and Unrat pretend not to have noticed. 'stehen lassen' = to leave standing (to walk away from someone). 'die Betäubung' = daze, numbness. 'die Konditorei' = cake shop and café – still very common in Germany and Austria ('der Konditor' = pastry chef). 'ein schlechtes Gewissen haben' = to have a guilty conscience. 'versöhnen' = to reconcile. 'das Büfett' = counter, buffet. 'sich hüten' = to take care not to.

units.en: That evening Unrat is restless and keeps saying 'Nothing here belongs to me but a sofa cushion and a picture frame.' Then he tells Rosa a secret: he has bribed Consul Breetpoot's cashier and found out that Breetpoot has been stealing the money he was supposed to look after for von Ertzum – so Ertzum will be ruined too. Kieselack is already destroyed, von Ertzum will be next; 'only the third remains to be caught.' He means Lohmann. 'But not you,' he begs Rosa strangely, 'you must not catch him!' Rosa thinks he has a fever. The next morning she spends two and a half hours getting dressed, finds an errand in town and stops in front of a bookshop – where she has never stopped before – feeling a nervous tingle at the back of her neck.

units.de:
»Gnädige Frau? Sieht man sich mal wieder?«
Sie zwang sich, indem sie sich wendete, zu anmutiger Langsamkeit in der Bewegung.
»Ach? Herr Lohmann? Sind Sie auch wieder im Lande?«
»Wenn ich dadurch nicht Ihr Missfallen errege, gnädige Frau?«
»Wieso denn. Aber wo haben Sie bloß Ihren Freund gelassen?«
»Sprechen Sie vom Grafen Ertzum? Nun, der hat seine eigenen Wege ... Aber gehn wir nicht weiter, gnädige Frau?«
»So? Und was macht er denn für gewöhnlich, Ihr Freund?«
»Er dient als Avantageur, gnädige Frau. Augenblicklich weilt er auf Urlaub hier.«
»Ach nee, was Sie sagen. Is er denn noch so nett wie früher?«
units.en:
'Madam? Do we meet again?'
As she turned, she forced herself to move with graceful slowness.
'Oh? Herr Lohmann? Are you back in the country too?'
'If that doesn't displease you, madam?'
'Why should it? But where on earth have you left your friend?'
'Are you talking about Count Ertzum? Well, he goes his own way ... But shall we walk on, madam?'
'Oh? And what does he usually do, your friend?'
'He's serving as an officer cadet, madam. At the moment he's here on leave.'
'Oh really, you don't say. Is he still as nice as he used to be?'
units.explain_en: Lohmann, now a polished young man, speaks to Rosa with exaggerated politeness. 'Gnädige Frau' = 'Madam' – a very formal old address, today only heard jokingly or in Austria. 'Sieht man sich mal wieder?' = do we meet again? 'wieder im Lande sein' = to be back home – still used jokingly. 'das Missfallen erregen' = to displease. 'der Avantageur' = officer cadet (old military term; today 'der Fahnenjunker'). 'auf Urlaub sein' = to be on leave/holiday. 'Ach nee, was Sie sagen' = oh really, you don't say.

units.en: In a café Lohmann tells Rosa his theory about Unrat: he is a tyrant who cannot bear being mocked and would rather destroy a whole town. Rosa invites Lohmann to visit her that afternoon, when Unrat is out. Rosa, who wants him precisely because he is the only man Unrat forbids, remembers the old days at the Blue Angel and starts to sing Lohmann's old song 'Der Mond ist rund' – the one song she must never sing. Suddenly the door crashes open and Unrat leaps into the room. Believing his worst fear has come true, he grabs Rosa by the throat. Lohmann pulls him away, and Rosa escapes and locks herself in the next room. Unrat, beside himself, snatches Lohmann's wallet and runs out. Shocked by these real crimes, Lohmann goes to the police.

units.de:
Ein Stündchen verrann; dann wälzte sich ein immer noch anschwellender Haufe um die Straßenecke. Die Stadt war in Jubel, weil Unrats Verhaftung beschlossen war. Endlich! Der Druck ihres eigenen Lasters ward von ihr genommen, da die Gelegenheit dazu entfernt ward. Man warf, zu sich kommend, einen Blick auf die Leichen ringsumher und entdeckte, dass es höchste Zeit sei. Warum man eigentlich so lange gewartet hatte.
Ein Bierwagen, hoch voll Fässern, versperrte schon die halbe Straße, da musste noch eine Droschke hindurch; und darin kamen die Beamten. Die Obstfrau von der Ecke lief mit; Herr Dröge, der Krämer, schleppte den Gummischlauch herbei.
units.en:
An hour passed; then an ever-growing crowd came rolling round the street corner. The town was rejoicing, because Unrat's arrest had been decided. At last! The weight of its own vice was lifted from it, since the opportunity for it was being removed. Coming to its senses, the town looked at the corpses all around and found that it was high time. Why on earth had they waited so long?
A brewer's cart, piled high with barrels, was already blocking half the street, and a cab still had to get through: in it came the officials. The fruit seller from the corner ran along too; Herr Dröge, the grocer, dragged up his rubber hose.
units.explain_en: The final chapter: the town that happily joined in Unrat's parties now celebrates his arrest. 'die Verhaftung' = arrest. 'das Laster' = vice, bad habit. 'die Gelegenheit' = opportunity. 'zu sich kommen' = to come to one's senses; also: to regain consciousness. 'die Leichen' = corpses – here meaning the people ruined by the scandal, not real dead bodies. 'höchste Zeit' = high time – very common. 'die Droschke' = horse-drawn cab (today: das Taxi). 'der Krämer' = old word for a small grocer.

units.de:
Vor Unrats Hause johlte das Gedränge. Endlich erschien er, inmitten der Beamten. Die Künstlerin Fröhlich, wirr, zerzaust, ganz in Tränen, zuckendem Jammer, Reue und unerhörter Unterworfenheit, klammerte sich an ihn, lag über ihn hingehängt, löste sich auf in ihn. Sie war mitverhaftet worden, was Lohmann nicht vorausgesehen hatte. Unrat hob sie in den geschlossenen Wagen, der ganz verfinstert war mit Gardinen; und er suchte zerfahren umher im Geheul. Einer hinterm Lederschurz, der Bierkutscher, reckte seinen bleichen Schlingelkopf heraus und quäkte:
»'ne Fuhre Unrat!«
units.en:
In front of Unrat's house the crowd was jeering. At last he appeared, surrounded by the officials. The artiste Fröhlich – confused, dishevelled, all in tears, in twitching misery, remorse and unheard-of submissiveness – clung to him, hung draped over him, dissolved into him. She had been arrested too, which Lohmann had not foreseen. Unrat lifted her into the closed carriage, which was made completely dark by curtains; and he looked around distractedly in the howling. One of the men behind a leather apron, the brewer's drayman, stretched his pale, rascally head out and squawked:
''A cartload of Unrat!'
units.explain_en: Rosa stays with Unrat to the end. 'johlen' = to jeer, to howl. 'zerzaust' = dishevelled, tousled. 'die Reue' = remorse, regret. 'sich klammern an' = to cling to. 'mitverhaftet' = arrested as well. 'vorhersehen' = to foresee. 'die Gardine' = curtain – still common. 'der Schlingel' = rascal (today used affectionately for naughty children). 'quäken' = to squawk. The last cry is a pun: 'eine Fuhre Unrat' = a cartload of rubbish.

units.de: Unrat warf sich herum, nach dem Wort, das nun kein Siegeskranz mehr war, sondern wieder ein ihm nachfliegendes Stück Schmutz – und erkannte Kieselack. Er schüttelte die Faust, er schnappte, den Hals vorgestreckt, in die Luft: aber Herrn Dröges Strahl prallte ihm grade in den Mund. Er sprudelte Wasser, empfing von hinten einen Stoß, stolperte das Trittbrett hinan und gelangte kopfüber auf das Polster neben der Künstlerin Fröhlich und in Dunkel.
units.en: Unrat spun round towards the word, which was no longer a victor's wreath but once again a piece of dirt flying after him – and recognised Kieselack. He shook his fist, he snapped at the air with his neck stretched out: but Herr Dröge's jet of water hit him right in the mouth. He spluttered water, received a shove from behind, stumbled up the step and landed head first on the seat beside the artiste Fröhlich, and in darkness.
units.explain_en: The last sentence of the novel: the old pupil Kieselack shouts the name, and Unrat is 'caught' at last. For a while Unrat had worn his name proudly like a 'Siegerkranz' (victor's wreath); now it is dirt again. 'sich herumwerfen' = to spin round. 'erkennen' = to recognise. 'die Faust schütteln' = to shake one's fist. 'der Strahl' = jet (of water); ray (of light). 'das Trittbrett' = running board, step of a carriage. 'kopfüber' = head first. The novel ends with the single word 'Dunkel' (darkness).
